title: Decadal biogeochemical predictions for the changing  bottom marine environment of the Gulf of Maine
content:
Decadal biogeochemical predictions for the changing bottom marine environment of the Gulf of Maine
Vimal Koul, Andrew C. Ross, Charles Stock, Liping Zhang, Andrew T. Wittenberg, and Thomas Delworth
Ocean Sci., 22, 3017–3036, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3017-2026, 2026
Predicting coastal ocean conditions years ahead has been difficult due to complex regional dynamics. This work shows we can forecast bottom temperature, oxygen, and acidity up to a decade ahead for the Northeast US Shelf. Our forecasts indicate increasing Labrador water may accelerate acidification, threatening shell-forming organisms. This provides a foundation for early warning systems to help communities and fisheries adapt proactively.

title: ProteomeScout v4: An open-source, harmonized, ecosystem for post-translational modifications
content: There are many databases of post-translational modifications, but each has different protein and PTM coverage, making the current state of post-translational modifications difficult to obtain, assess, or harmonize. ProteomeScout has been a relational database that harmonized a myriad of resources to address this challenge. In this update, we wished to create a lightweight, sustainable open source resource for the community that retained the power of harmonization, protein visualization, and Python tools for interacting with the database. ProteomeScout-v4 presents an ecosystem of open-source tools for aggregating and updating proteins and post-translational modifications and presenting the web-based and code-based access tools for interacting with the data. ProteomeScout has moved from using a complex relational database to a flat-text file format. The database file update is version controlled on FigShare and all features have processes for continuous updating, including migrating PTMs to updated protein records, when external databases are updated. The open-source nature and flexibility allow for user-based control and community-based feature integration. Fast and easy analysis is possible with the API, with example analyses provided here.

title: A quantitative interactome map reveals affinity tailored hijacking of human cellular functions by resident and pathogenic bacteria
content: Bacteria employ molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular functions for their own benefit. Despite the wealth of data mapping human-bacteria interactions, a comprehensive view of how these networks are fine-tuned remains elusive. In particular, there have been no large-scale screenings measuring human-bacterial protein-protein binding affinities to explore their role in functional and pathological outcomes. Here, we report the largest quantitative interactome to date between the family of human PDZ domains and C-terminal PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) in effectors from pathogenic and resident gut bacteria. We show that bacteria tailor effector sequences to bind PDZ domains with similar or higher binding affinities than human PBMs to hijack their associated cellular functions. For a subset of the dataset, we validate PDZ-PBM interactions with the corresponding full-length proteins and show that for pathogenic E. coli effector NleA, its C-terminal PBM is necessary for interactions with proteins involved in intracellular transport and membrane organization, probably impacting the host glycocalyx to favor infection. Finally, we show that motifs overlapping with effector PBMs target interaction modules other than PDZ domains, adding an additional layer of complexity to the host-microbe molecular dialogue.

title: Mucosal architecture, microbiota resilience and metabolic disruption reveal holobiont dynamics during bovine respiratory disease
content: The gut-airway axis is increasingly recognised as an important determinant of respiratory health in livestock. However, the interactions among respiratory infections, microbial communities, mucosal barrier function, and microbial metabolism that underpin this axis remain poorly understood. Here, we combined longitudinal immunological, mucosal, microbiological, and metabolic analyses to characterise host-microbiota interactions during antibiotic treatment and experimental bovine respiratory disease (BRD). We found that the bovine respiratory tract is organised as a hierarchically structured mucosal ecosystem, with compartment-specific mucin expression patterns associated with distinct microbial communities. Within this framework, increasing respiratory pathogen loads were associated with greater clinical severity, oxidative stress, acute inflammation, and targeted alterations in mucosal regulation and microbial composition, while serum amyloid A emerged as the host biomarker most closely reflecting infection intensity. Although infection altered host and microbial states, antimicrobial treatment represented the dominant ecological perturbation. Antibiotic exposure reshaped both respiratory and intestinal microbial communities, reducing diversity, increasing community drift, and driving coordinated ecological transitions across the gut-airway axis that exceeded the effects of infection alone. Importantly, these compositional changes were accompanied by profound reductions in acetate, propionate, butyrate, and valerate, identifying short-chain fatty acids as a major functional consequence of gut microbiota disruption. Integrative multi-omics analyses revealed that mucosal organisation, microbial diversity, microbial metabolism, and immune activity were embedded within a highly structured gut-airway network. Together, these findings support a holobiont view of BRD in which disease outcomes emerge not only from pathogen-host interactions but also from ecological disturbances that propagate across interconnected mucosal compartments. Notably, antimicrobial treatment affected ecosystem structure and function more than infection itself, highlighting potential trade-offs between pathogen control and microbiota stability. Preserving microbial resilience and its metabolic functions may therefore represent an important component of future strategies to improve respiratory health and disease resilience in cattle.

title: Scalable and semi-automated Boolean network inference from multi-condition single-cell transcriptomes with scBOLT
content: Predictive logical models have made substantial contributions to biomedical research by facilitating the identification of regulatory mechanisms driving biological processes. Yet, their construction remains a major bottleneck, as it typically relies on extensive prior knowledge at the genome scale. The emergence of high-throughput omics technologies has opened new opportunities for data-driven logical model construction by providing high-resolution observations of biological states. In parallel, formal constraint-based approaches have emerged, reformulating executable model inference as a constraint-satisfaction problem. However, transforming omics observations into biologically meaningful Boolean state abstractions and dynamical constraints suitable for logical synthesis engines remains challenging, particularly for poorly understood biological systems and multi-condition experimental settings. To address these challenges, we introduce scBOLT, a semi-automated framework for Boolean constraint engineering and logical model inference from multi-condition single-cell transcriptomes. Beyond these methodological contributions, scBOLT substantially improves computational tractability, enabling the inference of Boolean networks comprising several hundred components within practical runtimes.

title: Assay coverage reshapes metabolic diagnosis and the interpretation of pathway disturbance
content: Metabolic profiles are used to quantify disturbance, classify disease and infer biochemical function, yet these endpoints retain different information. We combine secondary analysis of 386 metabolites in six Arabidopsis thaliana mutation accumulation lines, known-disease classification in 129 public human metabolic-disease profiles, and an analytically solvable kinetic model. A conditional occupancy model separates annotation-bin breadth from hit count and measured bin sizes: the plant low-versus-high fitness comparison changes from a two-sided exact permutation p = 0.10 to p = 0.30 after calibration. Unsigned metabolite profiles achieve mean macro recall of 0.911 and 0.895 in separate EDTA and heparin subsets, compared with 0.624 and 0.382 for a burden baseline. However, controlled loss of 50% of held-out measurements reverses representation ranking in heparin, giving signed profiles a recall advantage of 0.108 with a conditional bootstrap interval of 0.063-0.155. A spectral decomposition identifies the within-pathway contrasts attenuated by smoothing. The kinetic model then shows that lower concentration and faster relaxation can coexist with reduced desired product flux, while a null-space criterion states when observations identify a metabolic task. The results connect assay coverage, diagnostic information and functional identifiability. Human performance is internally validated, and the kinetic predictions remain uncalibrated to patients.

title: Organizing principles of the cellular electron economy
content: Life runs on electron flow. Cells extract electrons from nutrients and transfer them through metabolism, coupling carbon use to energy conservation, biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. Yet how and even whether electron flow is organized at the system-level across metabolism remain unknown. Here we formalize the concept of the cellular electron economy: a quantitative, genome-wide, reaction-resolved representation of electron generation, transfer and disposal. This electron-centric perspective reveals a quantitative relationship governed by two distinct organizing factors: the carbon source sets the baseline and maximal rate of electron flow, whereas the capacity to dispose of electrons to terminal sinks determines where within this range the system operates. Carbon uptake can even increase as net electron flux falls. This system-level organization is shown to apply to five microorganisms with different intracellular electron routing pathways and predicts graded physiological responses to oxygen supply across carbon sources and respiratory architectures. The cellular electron economy thus links reaction-level redox chemistry to whole-cell metabolic organization and reveals how the same organizing principles govern electron flow across diverse metabolic architectures.

title: Comparative functional genomics of six Pectobacterium species reveals core and unique fitness determinants in potato tubers
content: Pectobacterium, a member of the soft rot Pectobacteriaceae (SRP), can cause highly destructive soft rot and blackleg diseases on many important crop and other host plants, particularly potato (Solanum tuberosum). Pectobacterium and its sister genus Dickeya have common virulence strategies, yet a highly diverse "open" pangenome containing many unique and hypothetical proteins. Here, we used randomly-barcoded transposon insertion-site sequencing (RB-TnSeq) on six Pectobacterium species to identify genes involved in bacterial survival and growth in potato tubers, as well as in minimal media conditions containing different single carbon sources. The strains evaluated varied broadly in genomic content as well as host plant and year of isolation. We focused on identifying conditionally essential genes across all strains tested, as well as genes that were important for growth in one or few of the tested strains. These results highlight the importance of many common genes involved in metabolism and maintaining cellular homeostasis, as well as shared and rare virulence traits including polygalacturonate catabolism, genes involved in polysaccharide biosynthesis, immunity proteins, and (for P. brasiliense) self-tolerance of the antibiotic carbapenem. This large dataset of conditionally essential genes, generated across Pectobacterium species during soft rot infection of the agriculturally important plant host potato, can serve as a rich dataset for further hypothesis generation and identification of important and/or novel in planta fitness factors.

title: Structure-Informed Stress-Testing of the Standard Numbering Scheme for Class B β-Lactamases Using AlphaFold2
content: The standard numbering scheme for class B beta-lactamases (metallo-beta-lactamases, MBLs), the BBL scheme, was proposed by Galleni et al. in 2001 and updated by Garau et al. in 2004 from the small number of MBL structures then solved. Hundreds of additional class B sequences have since been catalogued, but most have never been structurally solved, so whether BBL correspondences hold across this larger diversity has not been directly tested. Following the precedent set for the sibling class D enzymes, we used ColabFold (AlphaFold2/MMseqs2) to model 87 class B families across subclasses B1, B2, and B3 lacking an experimental structure, after validating the pipeline against an eight-enzyme benchmark spanning all three subclasses (RMSD to experimental structures 0.35-0.46 A). Applying BBL zinc-ligand numbering to the 87 models via paired sequence- and structure-based residue-transfer methods, the canonical zinc-coordination motif transferred cleanly in the large majority of families, and 11 of the 16 sequence-level exceptions were accounted for by a literature-supported biological cause (a subclass-appropriate substitution or a previously proposed, unconfirmed fourth subgroup), while two motif-retaining families showed predicted local structural divergence at the active-site loop, flagged by structural superposition, that could not be resolved to exact zinc-ligand numbering and warrants direct experimental follow-up. These results show that the BBL scheme, formulated before metagenomic sequencing or deep-learning structure prediction existed, generalizes robustly into the structural space these technologies have since opened, and identify a small set of variants whose active sites merit experimental attention.

title: Hiding in plain sight: rare Bacillus cereus group species are present among unassembled metagenomic samples in public databases
content: Abstract The Bacillus cereus group is a complex of closely related species, which vary in terms of their geographic spread, industrial utility, and pathogenic potential. In addition to encompassing well-known species represented by thousands of genomes (e.g., bioterrorism agent B. anthracis, foodborne pathogen B. cereus, biopesticide B. thuringiensis), the B. cereus group houses "rare" species discovered/first sequenced over a decade ago. Until recently, four rare species (B. manliponensis, B. bingmayongensis, B. gaemokensis, "B. clarus") were each represented by a single unique genome; as such, virtually nothing is known about these species beyond their type strains. We hypothesized that additional representatives of rare B. cereus group species may already be present in public databases as yet-unassembled metagenomes. To this end, we used species-specific markers to identify 7 metagenomic samples in NCBI's Sequence Read Archive, which harbored B. manliponensis, B. bingmayongensis, or B. gaemokensis. Metagenomic assembly and binning yielded an isolate-quality B. manliponensis metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) from avocado orchard soil in Israel, plus a partial B. bingmayongensis MAG from commercial spinach spiked with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli. For rare species represented by >1 unique genome, we compared our novel MAGs to all available genomes and identified strain- and lineage-specific genomic elements (e.g., sphingomyelinase C and hemolysin BL homologs, variably present in B. manliponensis and B. bingmayongensis, respectively). Altogether, our study indicates that some rare B. cereus group species may be more common and geographically widespread than previously thought, and highlights the utility of culture-independent methods for recovering rare/under-isolated taxa. Impact Statement Individual B. cereus group strains vary in terms of their pathogenic potential and industrial utility. While some strains cause illness in humans and/or animals (e.g., anthrax, emetic intoxication, diarrheal toxicoinfection, non-gastrointestinal illnesses), other strains have important biotechnological applications (e.g., biocontrol, plant growth promotion, production of antimicrobials and other natural products). Because many virulence- and biotechnological-related phenotypes are strain-dependent (rather than species-dependent), phenotypes associated with an individual strain (e.g., a species type strain) cannot be extrapolated to an entire B. cereus group species. Within this context, rare B. cereus group species represent a major gap in our understanding of B. cereus group evolution, ecology, and pathogenicity, as until 2021, each rare species was represented solely by its type strain genome. Here, we aggregate all publicly available genomes/MAGs of rare B. cereus group species and supplement them with their first novel representatives since 2024. Our efforts bring the total number of unique B. manliponensis and B. bingmayongensis genomes/MAGs to >2, allowing us to conduct the first-ever phylogeographic survey and strain-level assessment of functional potential for each species. Overall, our study represents a critical first step toward understanding rare B. cereus group species beyond their type strains.

title: A streamlined and abundant Nitrosopumilus population retains vitamin biosynthesis under high purifying selection in the Baltic Sea
content: Genome streamlining is expected to favor the loss of costly biosynthetic functions, raising the question of what benefit justifies the continued maintenance of complex pathways in small genomes. Here, we investigated this question in an abundant Nitrosopumilus population from the Baltic Sea that combined a streamlined genome (1.4 Mbp) with substantial biosynthetic capacity for vitamins B1, B7, and B12. We found three lines of evidence that support the biological significance of this retention. First, phylogenomic analysis of 1,077 archaeal species representatives showed that B-vitamin biosynthesis is broadly conserved across ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA), indicating maintenance over deep evolutionary timescales. Second, genes associated with B-vitamin biosynthesis tended to be under stronger purifying selection than the genomic background across Baltic Sea metagenomes, consistent with selection preserving these functions in current environmental populations. Third, measurements in the cultured relative Nitrosopumilus maritimus showed B-vitamins and related precursors in both intracellular and extracellular fractions, providing a potential route through which these retained functions could influence metabolite availability beyond the producing cell. Together, our findings suggest that retained biosynthetic pathways in highly streamlined microorganisms reveal functions that are beneficial for the success of a natural population, while also pointing to their potential importance for other community members coexisting within the same environment.

title: A Seed-Derived Multi-Kingdom Synthetic Community Enhances Radish Seedling Protection Against Alternaria brassicicola Abra43
content: Seed-associated microorganisms represent a promising resource for developing microbiome-based strategies against seed-borne pathogens. Here, we assembled synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) from cultivable members of the natural radish seed microbiota and evaluated their capacity to protect seedlings against the seed-transmitted fungal pathogen Alternaria brassicicola Abra43. Seven SynComs representing single- or multi-kingdom combinations of bacteria (B), filamentous fungi (F), and yeasts (Y) (B, F, Y, BF, BY, FY, and BFY) were inoculated onto radish seeds. We assessed their effects on disease incidence, seedling growth, microbial community assembly (ITS1 and gyrB gene metabarcoding) and pathogen colonization (metabarcoding and specific qPCR on dhn1 gene for A. brassicicola Abra43). Protection of radish seedlings against A. brassicicola Abra43 strongly depended on SynCom composition. The yeast fraction alone provided little protection, whereas the bacterial fraction partially reduced symptoms and maintained seedling growth despite substantial pathogen colonization, suggesting increased plant tolerance. SynComs containing filamentous fungi markedly reduced A. brassicicola Abra43 abundance, and the full multi-kingdom BFY SynCom provided the most consistent protection, combining reduced disease incidence, restored seedling growth, and low pathogen relative and absolute abundance. Inoculated strains, Alternaria alternata ABAI001 and Plectosphaerella sp. FL19 were enriched in protective SynComs and displayed antagonistic activity against A. brassicicola Abra43 in vitro. Together, these results show that seed-derived multi-kingdom communities can reshape early plant microbiota and that combining bacterial and fungal strains with complementary ecological functions can improve protection against a seed-borne fungal pathogen.

title: Bacterial NDH-1 is a key gut target of metformin mediating its antidiabetic effects
content: Metformin is the first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes, yet the mechanisms underlying its glucose-lowering effects remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence implicates gut microbiota as an important mediator of metformin action, but the bacterial targets of the drug remain poorly defined. Here, we identify bacterial NADH oxidoreductase (NDH-1), the homolog of mitochondrial complex I, as a key target of metformin. Metformin inhibited bacterial growth at millimolar concentrations and, at subinhibitory concentrations, markedly impaired carbohydrate fermentation in Escherichia coli and other NDH-1-containing bacteria. Supplementation with nicotinic acid and Mg2+; restored fermentation, whereas pyruvate bypassed the metabolic defect, implicating impaired NAD+; regeneration and disruption of metabolism upstream of pyruvate formation. Genetic analysis further established NDH-1 dependence: metformin failed to inhibit fermentation in an E. coli delta-nuoF mutant lacking functional NDH-1 but retained activity in an NDH-2-deficient delta-ndh strain. Molecular docking predicted metformin binding within the NDH-1 quinone-binding region, proximal to conserved residues involved in quinone reduction. Consistent with this mechanism, Staphylococcus aureus, which lacks NDH-1, was not affected in carbohydrate fermentation, while several gut-associated probiotic and short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Akkermansia muciniphila, lacked detectable NDH-1 homologs, suggesting intrinsic resistance to this metabolic effect of metformin. These findings identify bacterial NDH-1 as a metabolic target of metformin and provide a mechanistic framework for its effects on the gut microbiota. Selective inhibition of NDH-1-dependent bacteria could alter microbial substrate utilization and ecological interactions in the intestine, potentially contributing to the microbiome-mediated component of metformin's antidiabetic effects.

title: Effects of CO2 on the growth and metabolism of Akkermansia muciniphila
content: The human gut is home to more than 100 trillion bacteria, where various environmental factors, such as nutrients and gases, exist and influence them. The levels of fermentation gases in the gut, including CO2, fluctuate depending on the host's diet. However, how CO2, an environmental factor, affects the physiological states of gut anaerobes remains poorly understood, but CO2 is often utilized in their cultivation. Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila) is widely studied as a beneficial human gut microbe. However, the effects of CO2 on the physiological state of A. muciniphila are not fully understood. In this study, we focused on CO2 as an environmental factor and aimed to clarify how CO2 affects the physiological state of A. muciniphila. Culture experiments showed that compared with the absence of CO2, the presence of CO2 significantly increased the growth of A. muciniphila. The results of the metabolomic analysis revealed distinct metabolic profiles in the presence or absence of CO2. The tracing analysis using stable 13C-labelled CO2 demonstrated that CO2 was incorporated into various metabolites in the TCA cycle, the de novo purine/pyrimidine synthesis pathways, and other pathways. In addition, the activity of pyruvate carboxylase, which catalyses an anaplerotic reaction involving CO2 fixation to supply oxaloacetate (OAA) to the TCA cycle, was significantly higher in A. muciniphila cells grown in the presence of CO2. Moreover, supplementation with OAA increased the growth of A. muciniphila in a dose-dependent manner, mirroring the effects of CO2 supplementation. These findings suggest that A. muciniphila utilizes CO2 for an anaplerotic reaction in the TCA cycle and other pathways involving CO2 incorporation, facilitating metabolic flux to promote its robust growth.

title: Evidence of active phage replication during vegetable fermentation and implications for the dynamics of bacterial communities
content: Spontaneous vegetable fermentation is driven by the indigenous microbiota associated with the raw ingredients. The process often involves an initial heterofermentative phase followed by a predominantly homofermentative phase, both ensured by lactic acid bacteria (LAB). While microbial dynamics during fermentation are well characterized, phage communities remain poorly understood, despite evidence linking phage activity to LAB succession. We monitored viral and bacterial succession during sauerkraut and carrot fermentations using a metagenomics approach to characterize community dynamics. To further assess the impact of phage PLE001 on bacterial community dynamics, we developed a simplified carrot fermentation model comprising representative strains of Rahnella aquatilis, Leuconostoc mesenteroides and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum. Two consortia were assembled: one containing the PLE001-susceptible strain L. mesenteroides CIM3004, and the other containing also its phage-resistant derivative, CIM3004 BIM. We observed major shifts in the viral community during the first week of fermentation, coinciding with changes in bacterial structure during hetero- and homofermentative phases transition. In the simplified model, phage PLE001 reduced the population of the host during the heterofermentative phase but did not affect overall fermentation dynamics nor metabolite production. These results suggest that bacteriophages contribute to bacterial succession during fermentation, while communities remain resilient to phage infection, preserving fermentation stability.

title: Codon usage bias maps ocean microbiome adaptation to temperature-nutrients regimes
content: Microbial communities underpin ocean productivity and biogeochemistry, but their functional adaptation to environmental gradients remains poorly understood. Codon usage bias (CUB), a marker of translational efficiency, constrains growth rate potential, yet its role in functional adaptation across natural communities is underexplored. By analysing 589 metagenome-derived microbial communities from the global ocean, we demonstrate that CUB in 320 metabolism-related gene groups capture genomic adaptation to distinct temperature and nutrient concentrations. We identified four adaptation signatures shaped by distinct temperature-nutrient regimes, revealing how microbes optimize protein synthesis in their ecological niche. This genome-centric approach deepens our understanding of functional adaptation in uncultured marine microbes and provides a framework to inform ocean biogeochemical models and predict microbial responses to climate-driven changes.

title: Host Cellular Remodeling, Not Viral Transcriptional Inhibition, Drives Quorum Sensing Signal-Mediated Evasion of Viral Lysis in Gephyrocapsa huxleyi
content: Bacterial infochemicals can profoundly alter phytoplankton physiology, yet how these compounds influence viral infection outcomes remains poorly understood. The bacterial quorum sensing molecule 2-heptyl-4-quinolone (HHQ) enables the globally abundant coccolithophore, Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, to evade virus-induced mortality following infection by Emiliania huxleyi virus (EhV). HHQ reduced infectious virus production at 24 hours despite largely intact viral gene transcription, as revealed by RNA sequencing of host and viral responses during EhV-201 infection. Host transcriptomics instead revealed rapid and progressive HHQ-dependent physiological remodeling evidenced by changes in protein encoding genes associated with vesicular trafficking, and cytoskeletal organization. Transcriptional responses further implicated endolysosomal sorting, membrane remodeling, and protein modification as potential barriers to productive infection. These findings indicate that HHQ-mediated evasion of virus-induced mortality occurs downstream of viral entry and transcription, through remodeling of host processes required for virion assembly, maturation, trafficking, and release.

title: Restoring Antibiotic Sensitivity via Metabolic Pathway Manipulation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
content: Stopping antimicrobial multidrug resistance (AMR) is essential to maintain the efficacy of current treatments and sustain modern medicine, but current control relies on a coordinated One Health approach involving stewardship, infection prevention and other control measures, without direct actionable mechanisms against resistance itself. Here, integrating proteomics and metabolomics with high-throughput Caenorhabditis elegans infection models, we show that unique synergy of biotin biosynthesis inhibition with metformin uncouples virulence from bacterial viability shutting down major Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) virulence mechanisms that impair host survival. Under directed evolution induced by central carbon metabolic stress, laboratory and clinical PA strain isolates acquire mutations in the MexAB-OprM multidrug efflux pump, leading to reversal of the AMR phenotype and restored susceptibility to multiple legacy and last-resort antibiotics such as meropenem. Our findings reveal a previously unexploited vulnerability in PA, its co-dependence on biotin biosynthesis and energy metabolism for virulence and resistance. This work establishes a conceptual framework in which metabolic co-targeting can abolish pathogenesis and drive reversal of antimicrobial resistance. It lays the foundation for first-in-class, non-antibiotic PA-selective anti-virulence and resistance-reversing therapies, key to extending the lifesaving duration of existing antibiotics.

title: Structural mechanism of metal-induced DNA release by an ArsR/SmtB transcriptional regulator
content: Metal-responsive transcriptional regulators must couple metal coordination to DNA release at the DNA-binding interface. However, the pathway connecting these states remains poorly understood. Here, we define this mechanism for the ArsR/SmtB-family repressor CadC from Listeria monocytogenes by combining crystal structures of apo, DNA-bound, and cadmium-bound states with biochemical and in vivo analyses. The DNA-bound structure reveals how CadC dimers bind sequence-specifically to operator DNA, via coordinated major-groove, wing and backbone interactions, with high-affinity binding depending on operator architecture. Cadmium is coordinated at the 3N sensor by an unusual Cys3-Met ligand set and stabilizes a DNA-incompatible conformation through remodeling of DNA-contacting elements and steric incompatibility between the ordered N-terminus and DNA. Mutational analyses show how these structural transitions link to metal-dependent transcriptional control in Listeria cells. We show that CadC binds zinc and supports zinc-responsive transcription in bacterial cells, and that host zinc availability modifies CadC-dependent infection phenotypes. Together, results reveal how metal coordination is converted into DNA release through coupled allosteric remodeling and steric exclusion, establishing a mechanism for signal-dependent transcriptional switching in ArsR/SmtB metalloregulators.

title: RSV & rhinovirus coinfection order dictates outcome via type III interferon-mediated interference in infant respiratory epithelium
content: Coinfection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and rhinovirus (RV) is the most frequently detected coinfection in infants, yet mechanisms governing viral interference and disease outcome remain poorly understood. Although infection order is a key determinant of coinfection outcome involving RSV, influenza, rhinovirus, and SARS-CoV-2, its role in RSV/RV coinfections has not been defined. Using infant-derived human nasal organoids at air-liquid interface, we demonstrate that coinfection order fundamentally determines the outcome of RSV/RV interactions. An initial RSV infection almost completely inhibits secondary RV coinfection, whereas primary RV infection only partially impairs a subsequent RSV coinfection. These distinct outcomes are accompanied by divergent temporal antiviral and pro-inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, we identify type III interferons as a sufficient mediator of RSV-induced restriction of RV, establishing a host-driven mechanism of viral interference. In contrast, partial impairment of RSV following RV infection occurs through an interferon-independent mechanism. Despite marked differences, RSV/RV coinfections do not exacerbate epithelial injury or innate immune responses beyond that induced by RSV alone, indicating RSV is the dominant driver of pathology in coinfections. Collectively, our data establishes coinfection order as a critical determinant of RSV/RV outcome and reveals novel and mechanistic insight into critical viral-host interactions in the infant nasal epithelium.

title: Genomically and ecologically cohesive subspecies as biologically meaningful units in the global ocean microbiome
content: Microbial diversity is organised into operationally defined species. However, it remains unclear whether these, or finer-scale groups represent biologically meaningful units in natural communities. Here, we implement a scalable, cultivation-independent framework to identify 724 genomically discrete and ecologically cohesive subspecies across 270 species in the global ocean microbiome. Their diversification is underpinned by gene-specific, nucleotide-level selection on the core genomic backbone and by variable restructuring of gene content, both of which proceed in a subspecies-specific manner. In over half of the species tested, subspecies were significantly associated with distinct environmental conditions, most frequently temperature. This coupling of genomic discreteness and ecological cohesiveness positions these subspecies as biologically meaningful units, a fundamental level at which ecological and evolutionary processes jointly drive divergence and structure microbial diversity in the oceans.

title: Neoehrlichia mikurensis, where art thou? A negative analysis of 87 Swedish wild boars (Sus scrofa)
content: Neoehrlichia mikurensis is widely detected in tick populations across Europe, yet its host range beyond small rodents remains poorly understood. Large wild mammals are frequently exposed to tick vectors, but their role in the transmission cycle of this bacterium is unclear. Wild boars (Sus scrofa) are among the most abundant large mammals in southern Sweden and commonly inhabit tick-infested environments, making them a potentially relevant host species. In this study, spleen samples from 87 wild boars collected between 2023 and 2025 across southern and central Sweden were analysed for the presence of N. mikurensis DNA using quantitative polymerase chain reaction. N. mikurensis DNA was not detected in any of the analysed samples, despite sampling in regions where the bacterium is known to be prevalent in ticks. These results indicate that wild boars may have a limited role in the maintenance of N. mikurensis in Sweden, although the possibility of rare or transient infection cannot be excluded. Despite being based on negative findings, this study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the host range of N. mikurensis and highlights the importance of continued evaluation of wildlife species in the transmission dynamics of tick-borne pathogens.

title: Scale- and genotype-dependent spatial concordance of Mycobacterium bovis in cattle and badgers
content: Mycobacterium bovis causes tuberculosis (TB) in cattle, badgers (Meles meles), other wildlife, and humans, posing major animal and public health challenges in Britain and Ireland. Shared genotypes between cattle and badgers have been reported at regional scales, but whether this concordance holds at finer spatial scales, where control interventions operate, and whether it varies by genotype combination, remains unknown. Resolving this is critical for interpreting cross-species transmission risk and designing targeted control measures. We analyzed 1,248 M. bovis isolates from cattle and badgers (Northern Ireland, 1986-2018), including samples from a small, densely sampled intervention research area, using Multi-Locus Variable Number of Tandem Repeats Analysis (MLVA) and kernel discriminant analysis (KDA) across multiple spatial scales (25-95% density contours). We identified 36 MLVA types with four shared between species and one (MLV06) endemic to the area. Spatial concordance varied by type combination and scale: MLVA004-MLVA297 showed strong, bidirectional, scale-robust concordance; MLVA006-MLVA297 was concordant only at fine spatial scales; MLVA004-MLVA006 showed weak, asymmetric concordance; and no concordance was detected when all three types were analysed together. Our findings reveal spatial concordance between shared M. bovis genotypes varied by genotype combination and scale, indicating genotype-specific dynamics within this multi-host system.

title: Climate‐Linked Si‐Fe Dynamics and Their Associations With Soil Mineral‐Associated Organic Carbon
content:
Abstract
Iron (Fe) (hydr)oxides and silicate minerals are key controls on the formation of mineral‐associated organic carbon (MAOC) in soils—a relatively persistent fraction of soil organic carbon (SOC). Silicon (Si) is essential for silicate mineral formation, and the interactions between Fe and Si are widespread in natural environments. However, the interactive effects of Fe (hydr)oxides and Si on MAOC remain poorly understood. Here, we determined Fe and Si speciation in soils across diverse ecosystems by selective extraction, and estimated their individual and interactive effects on MAOC. Our results show that pedogenic and biogenic amorphous Si are positively associated with MAOC accumulation, while more mobile Si forms (including dissolved and weakly adsorbed Si) are negatively associated with the formation of Fe‐bound organic carbon (Fe‐OC). Although amorphous Fe oxides serve as the dominant carriers of Fe‐OC complexes, increasing metal oxide‐associated Si is linked to a reduced contribution of Fe oxides to MAOC. Additionally, temperature and precipitation are associated with variations in Si and Fe speciation, likely through changes in soil weathering stage and pH, and these patterns are further linked to differences in MAOC accumulation. Our results highlight climate‐linked Si‐Fe dynamics and interactions as critical but previously underappreciated factors related to SOC stabilization, and we suggest that Si speciation should be integrated into land management and SOC sequestration strategies across diverse ecosystems.

title: ‘Candidatus Viridifilum namsaraevi’ gen. nov., sp. nov., a new mesophilic filamentous anoxygenic phototrophic bacterium from the mesothermal lake Umkhey (Buryatia)
content:
Abstract
The evolution of phototrophy and carbon fixation in the phylum Chloroflexota remains incompletely understood, largely due to the scarcity of cultured mesophilic representatives. Here, we report the isolation and genomic characterization of a novel filamentous anoxygenic phototrophic bacterium from a microbial mat in the mesothermal Lake Umkhey (Southern Siberia). Although the original culture was lost, its genome was recovered via metagenome-assembled genome reconstruction from environmental samples, enabling a detailed phylogenomic and metabolic analysis. The genome of umkhey_bin13 (proposed as ‘Candidatus Viridifilum namsaraevi’ gen. nov., sp. nov.) encodes a complete 3-hydroxypropionate bicycle for autotrophic CO₂ fixation, a type II sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase, but lacks nitrogenase and chemolithotrophic markers. Comparative genomics across 18 Chloroflexota genomes reveals that this new lineage occupies an intermediate phylogenetic position, with distinct gene content for sulfur, nitrogen, and hydrogen metabolism, and highlights a complex evolutionary history within the group. Our findings provide new insights into the evolutionary transitions of photosynthetic and carbon-fixation pathways, and underscore the value of integrating cultivation-independent genomics with classical microbiology. The proposed novel genus and species contribute to a revised framework of Chloroflexota evolution and offer a genomic reference for studying metabolic adaptation in alkaline, sulfide-influenced microbial mats.

title: In the World of Aquatic Parasites, Microsporidia Matter!
content:
Microsporidia could exert a considerable influence in aquatic ecosystems, similar to the impact observed for other eukaryotic parasites. It is essential to continue expanding research on the diversity and ecological roles of Microsporidia.

ABSTRACT
Microsporidia are highly diverse, widespread parasites related to fungi and several groups of zoosporic protistan parasites. They infect a broad range of hosts, from protists to vertebrates, in many environments including most, if not all, aquatic habitats. Their genomes range from relatively conventional to highly reduced, yet they share key cellular structures and traits underlying infection and host association. Overall microsporidian diversity, including both ‘long‐branched’ and ‘short‐branched’ lineages, is poorly sampled; their environmental diversity and host range remain therefore largely unexplored. Although short sequences are often insufficient to distinguish between species, recent targeted metabarcoding studies have revealed unexpectedly high microsporidian diversity in both oceanic and lacustrine ecosystems, along with significant spatial and temporal variation. These studies have also identified several previously unrecognized hosts, including heterotrophic protists, phytoplankton and microzooplankton, all key components of the base of aquatic food webs. These findings suggest that Microsporidia, like other parasitic groups, may strongly influence the structure and functioning of aquatic ecosystems. We therefore advocate increased research on Microsporidia across aquatic habitats. Integrative research combining phylogenomics, long‐read sequencing and ecology studies will be essential to fully characterize their diversity, host associations and ecological impacts.

title: Quantifying hybrid electrochemical–biological CO₂ conversion systems

title: Solving calibration and reanalysis challenges of ocean biogeochemical dynamics with neural schemes: a 1D vertical model case-study
content:
Solving calibration and reanalysis challenges of ocean biogeochemical dynamics with neural schemes: a 1D vertical model case-study
Jean Littaye, Laurent Memery, and Ronan Fablet
Biogeosciences, 23, 6879–6914, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-6879-2026, 2026
A realistic representation of ocean carbon exchanges through a biogeochemical (BGC) model depends heavily on its parameterisation. However, this calibration is often hindered by an inaccurate representation of small-scale ocean physical dynamics, which are common in physical reanalysis. Here, a novel learning-based method enables a robust estimation of BGC states and parameters, and correction of physical forcing, despite physical forcing uncertainties and sparse observations.

title: Towards constraining the drivers of variability and trends in subantarctic productivity
content:
Towards constraining the drivers of variability and trends in subantarctic productivity
Christopher D. Traill, Tyler W. Rohr, Elizabeth H. Shadwick, Pearse J. Buchanan, Alessandro Tagliabue, and Andrew R. Bowie
Biogeosciences, 23, 6947–6977, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-6947-2026, 2026
Southern Ocean phytoplankton are a key part of the carbon cycle, yet year-to-year changes in ocean productivity are poorly understood. Using model simulations, this study shows how deeper mixing in the most productive years increases nutrient supply and changes the predator-prey relationship between phytoplankton and zooplankton. This helps explain why satellite productivity estimates disagree, and the reasons for why climate projections might be getting inaccurate estimates of future production.

title: Unlocking the air: DNA metabarcoding sheds light on seasonal fungal dynamics in a temperate floodplain forest
content:
Unlocking the air: DNA metabarcoding sheds light on seasonal fungal dynamics in a temperate floodplain forest
Ettore Fedele, Christina M. Müller, Volker Wissemann, Birgit Gemeinholzer, Christian Wirth, and Beatriz Sánchez-Parra
Biogeosciences, 23, 6931–6945, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-6931-2026, 2026
Fungi are key component of the air we breathe. They travel short and long distances, influencing ecosystems, agriculture and human health worldwide. Using advanced DNA techniques, we monitored airborne fungi in a European floodplain forest and linked their presence to climatic conditions. We found that temperature can shape airborne fungal communities, including the presence of allergenic and pathogenic fungi. This highlights the importance of long-term monitoring under climate change scenarios.

title: Summer oxygen dynamics in the bottom waters of a wide, temperate shelf sea
content:
Summer oxygen dynamics in the bottom waters of a wide, temperate shelf sea
Xin Meng, Claire Mahaffey, Juliane Wihsgott, and Jonathan Sharples
Biogeosciences, 23, 6915–6929, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-6915-2026, 2026
Summer oxygen loss in Celtic Sea bottom waters was investigated using ship observations and an oxygen budget. Seasonal layering cuts deep water off from the air, while microbes breaking down organic matter consume most oxygen. Winds can mix oxygen downward, but warming may worsen oxygen loss by speeding microbial activity and lowering oxygen solubility. This could push parts of the shelf sea toward oxygen deficiency, with risks for seafloor life and ecosystem health.

title: Surface Chlorophyll‐a Trends in the Mediterranean Sea: Seasonal Bloom Dynamics and Drivers
content:
Abstract
Chlorophyll‐a (Chl‐a) is the most widely used proxy for phytoplankton biomass, bloom intensity, and trophic status in marine ecosystems. We analyzed 27 years (1998–2024) of 1 km‐resolution satellite‐derived Chl‐a data across the Mediterranean Sea and evaluated long‐term trends, bloom phenology, and seasonal variability in relation to sea surface temperature, mixed‐layer depth, and nutrient dynamics. A Mediterranean‐specific Chl‐a algorithm was also used to accurately represent both open and optically complex coastal waters. Before assessing trends, we compared three central‐tendency metrics to account for the right‐skewed nature of Chl‐a distributions. The geometric mean best represents typical conditions by reducing the influence of extreme values and was therefore selected as it enhances the robustness of basin‐scale trend detection. Trend analysis revealed a basin‐wide decline in surface Chl‐a over the 27‐year study period, with negative trends across all seasons and localized increases in some coastal areas. The longer satellite record reconciles previously reported spatially heterogeneous trends. The clustering of Chl‐a variability delineated a gradient from productive, seasonally dynamic regions to persistently oligotrophic regimes. Regionally, the spring bloom magnitude declined in the Gulf of Lion (northwestern Mediterranean) and the southern Adriatic Sea, whereas biomass in the Levantine Sea (eastern basin) remained persistently low. Overall, these patterns suggest a shift toward increased oligotrophy, as warming‐induced stratification suppresses nutrient resupply. By combining long‐term satellite observations, robust Chl‐a statistics, and phenological analysis, this study provides an update and comprehensive assessment of phytoplankton variability and its drivers in the Mediterranean Sea.

title: Internal Tides, Non‐linear Internal Waves, and Mixing Over a Large River‐Dominated Inner Shelf
content:
Abstract
Internal waves (IWs) profoundly influence turbulent mixing in stratified coastal seas, yet their dynamics in large river‐dominated inner shelves remain poorly understood. With high‐frequency observations from bottom‐mounted tripods and stationary ship‐based platforms, this study provides the first comprehensive dynamical characterization of internal tides and high‐frequency non‐linear internal waves (NLIWs) in the Changjiang Estuary (CE). In summer, strong freshwater‐induced stratification supported an energetic IW field consisting of multi‐modal internal tides and frequent mode‐1 NLIWs. Modal analysis revealed that the observed “sandwich” velocity structure arose from the superposition of low‐ and high‐order modes with distinct phase velocities. NLIWs occurred two to three times per day, typically propagating southwestward in mode‐1 form, with the highest total kinetic‐energy flux exceeding 300 W m−1. Their passage enhanced turbulent dissipation (>10−5 W kg−1) and diffusivity (10−4–10−3 m2 s−1) near the pycnocline, driving intermittent but intense turbulence. Froude number analysis suggests that many NLIWs occurred during transitions from supercritical to subcritical flow, reminiscent of lee wave mechanism over steep slope. In contrast, winter observations showed weakened stratification, reduced baroclinic M2 flux (∼8% of summer), and the absence of NLIWs, while storm events dominated mixing in the upper water column. Collectively, these results highlight strong seasonal modulation of IW processes and underscore the controlling influence of stratification and topography on diapycnal mixing, which is critical for regulating nutrient fluxes and primary productivity across the East China Sea inner shelf.

title: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi mediated biotic carbon pump in alpine meadows of the Qinghai Tibetan Plateau under a warming and wetting climate: patterns and mechanism
content:
Abstract
Climate warming accompanied by an overall increase in precipitation has reshaped hydrothermal regimes in many alpine meadows on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, with important implications for soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics. However, precipitation trajectories are spatially heterogeneous across alpine meadow regions, and the direction and mechanisms underlying SOC responses to warming–wetting conditions remain uncertain. While traditional frameworks emphasize plant litter inputs, emerging evidence highlights the central role of microbial processes in SOC stabilization. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF), which are widely distributed in alpine meadow ecosystems, mediate plant-derived carbon (C) transfer into soils and may regulate SOC formation, turnover, and stabilization. This review synthesizes current knowledge on how warming and increased precipitation influence SOC stocks and dynamics in alpine meadows, with a focus on AMF-mediated mechanisms. We highlight how AMF regulate belowground C inputs, priming effects, and microbial metabolism, thereby affecting SOC accumulation and stabilization. Evidence indicates that warming and altered precipitation jointly modify SOC turnover by influencing plant–AMF C allocation, AMF community composition, microbial C use efficiency, and enzyme activities. These responses are strongly context dependent.We propose an AMF-mediated biotic C pump (BCP) under warming and wetting, emphasizing the role of AMF in promoting the incorporation and stabilization of newly fixed C in soils. This framework advances understanding of C cycling and improves predictions of ecosystem feedbacks to climate change.

title: Multidimensional Trait Space of Soil Protists: Ecological Strategies and Environmental Responses
content:
ABSTRACT
Soil protists comprise vast eukaryotic diversity and play key roles in microbial food webs, yet their community assembly remains poorly understood from a trait‐based perspective. Here, we address this gap by integrating 10 traits related to morphology, behaviour, life history and trophic strategy across broad environmental gradients. RLQ analysis combined with fourth‐corner tests revealed two major dimensions of soil protist trait variation. Reduced precipitation drove trait composition towards slower, persistence‐oriented strategies, including reduced mobility, narrower niche breadth and increased reliance on asexual reproduction. Nutrient and resource limitation shifted trophic structure away from heterotrophic consumer‐related strategies towards autotrophic or mixotrophic energy acquisition. These dimensions were consistently detected in a large‐scale field survey and broadly supported by an independent global‐change manipulation experiment, indicating that they capture generalizable components of soil protist functional organization. Further functional diversity analyses indicated that environmental gradients primarily constrained the range of occupied trait space rather than consistently reshaping the internal dispersion or evenness of trait distributions. Our study provides a trait‐based framework for predicting belowground community assembly and ecosystem functional responses to environmental change.

title: Warm springs compress budbreak, affecting floral freezing risk in red (Acer rubrum) and silver maple (A. saccharinum)
content:
Abstract
Red (Acer rubrum) and silver maple (Acer saccharinum) flower before leafing out in the early spring, making them vulnerable to post‐budbreak freezing (false springs), a risk climate change exacerbates. They also show interannual variation in fruit production (masting), but it is unknown whether this pattern is related to freezing damage after budbreak. We observed budbreak phenology and measured cold hardiness of floral and vegetative buds of both maple species from dormancy to spring budbreak in 2024 and 2025. We also collected buds three times in 2025, incubated them in growth chambers up to 22°C, and quantified their deacclimation velocity. Finally, we used regional phenological data to assess whether local variation in fruit production might depend on false spring risk. We established the physiological context of spring budbreak in our study species: Silver maple floral buds open first and when very cold hardy, need minimal chilling, and lose cold hardiness rapidly; red maple vegetative buds open last and when least cold hardy, need considerable chilling, and lose cold hardiness slowly; and red maple floral buds and silver maple vegetative buds are intermediate. Though low fruit production was found to correlate with warm March temperatures followed by late March cold spells, we did not find direct, mechanistic evidence that local cold weather killed floral buds, decreasing fruit production. Differential physiology of maple buds interacts with climate to determine phenology. Both study species are at low risk of false spring damage, although it is unclear whether and how variable spring weather affects masting dynamics.

title: Distributions of economically important nonindigenous forest pests in the conterminous United States
content:
Abstract
The geographical distributions of established nonindigenous forest insects and pathogens have historically not been well documented nor centrally aggregated, the absence of which has contributed to constrained efforts to manage and minimize resultant damages. To address this need, we present the construction of a centralized database accessible via a publicly available web portal, the Alien Forest Pest Explorer. All nonindigenous forest insect and pathogen species known to cause economic impacts in the conterminous U.S. were selected for inclusion in the database. The occurrence of these established pests, which is derived from a variety of data streams including reports by state and Federal agencies, the scientific literature, and biodiversity databases, is recorded at the county level. In addition to data on geographical distribution of the pests, the database also provides county‐level data that quantifies the volume of host trees species derived from forest inventory data. Overall, the data and analyses presented here provide baseline information regarding the distribution of nonindigenous forest pests and changes in host resources. Our database can also help to provide a more complete understanding of the impacts of nonindigenous forest pests on U.S. forests and can be used as a public resource in supporting regional invasive forest pest research and management. The data are available for reuse under CC0 1.0 Universal licensing; however, we appreciate the citation of this data paper when reusing the dataset.

title: Repurposing ritonavir to induce proteasomal degradation of IE1 for inhibition of human cytomegalovirus replication
content:
by Wanfeng Liu, Yu Shi, Xudong Guo, Chenyu Lou, Zhangyi Xie, Yitian Shen, Liang Zhang, Sunzhong Mao, Xiangyang Xue, Shiyu Feng

Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a major pathogen affecting immunocompromised individuals. Current antiviral drugs target the mid-to-late stages of viral replication but are limited by toxicity and drug resistance. The IE1 protein serves as a key early regulator of HCMV replication; however, it has long been considered undruggable due to the lack of conventional drug-binding sites. In this study, by integrating molecular docking-based virtual screening with in-vitro surface plasmon resonance (SPR) validation, we discovered for the first time that the HIV protease inhibitor ritonavir may bind to the IE1 protein. Further experiments demonstrated that ritonavir significantly reduces IE1 protein levels in a time- and dose-dependent manner without affecting its mRNA expression. Mechanistic investigations revealed that ritonavir promotes selective degradation of IE1 through activation of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Functional assays confirmed that ritonavir effectively inhibits HCMV replication, markedly reducing viral DNA loads and the production of infectious viral particles. Notably, ritonavir exhibited synergistic antiviral effects when combined with the first-line drug ganciclovir (GCV). In summary, this study successfully repurposes the approved drug ritonavir as a regulator of IE1 protein expression, demonstrating not only its anti-HCMV activity and synergistic effects with GCV but also providing a new therapeutic strategy for HCMV infection.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics As Rasterized Image Tensors (STARIT) characterizes cell states with subcellular molecular heterogeneity
content:
by Dee Velazquez, Caleb Hallinan, Roujin An, Kalen Clifton, Jean Fan

Imaging-based spatially resolved transcriptomics (imSRT) technologies provide high-throughput molecular-resolution spatial characterization of genes within cells. Conventional analysis methods to identify cell-types and states in imSRT data rely on gene count matrices derived from tallying the number of mRNA molecules detected for each gene per segmented cell, thereby overlooking subcellular heterogeneity that can be useful in defining cell states. To take advantage of the molecular-resolution information in imSRT data and potentially identify cell-states based on subcellular heterogeneity, we developed STARIT (Spatial Transcriptomics As Rasterized Image Tensors). STARIT converts transcripts within segmented cells in imSRT data into an image-based tensor representation that can be combined with deep learning computer vision models for downstream analysis. Using simulated and real imSRT data, we demonstrate that STARIT distinguishes transcriptionally distinct cell-types and further separates cell states based on subcellular transcript localization, which conventional gene count analysis fails to capture. By providing a standardized framework to encode subcellular molecular information in imSRT data, STARIT will enable deeper insights into subcellular heterogeneity and enhance the identification and characterization of cell-types and states that are overlooked by gene count representations.

title: Mobility hinders malaria elimination goals in the Brazilian Amazon
content:
by Nicholas J. Arisco, Pablo S. Fontoura, Cassio Peterka, Marcia C. Castro

Introduction

Human mobility across the Brazilian Amazon—shaped by frontier development, land-use change, mining activity, and climatic shocks—remains a major barrier to malaria elimination. Brazil aims to eliminate Plasmodium falciparum (Pf) by 2030 and Plasmodium vivax (Pv) by 2035, yet malaria incidence has plateaued since 2020. We quantify parasite-specific mobility and assess how importations drive malaria reintroduction and reestablishment in areas approaching elimination.

Methods

We analyzed 5,521,411 de-identified malaria cases from Sivep-Malaria (2003–2023) across 808 municipalities in the nine-state Brazilian Amazon. We (i) used multivariable monthly sequence analysis to classify “Municipal Malaria Importation Trajectories” (MMITs) using local/imported composition, incidence per 1,000, and source/sink network typologies; (ii) characterized mobility networks by parasite species and locality type (rural, urban, settlement, indigenous, mining); and (iii) developed a parasite-specific rule-based classification procedure to identify reintroduction, and defined reestablishment as sustained local transmission.

Results

Sequence analysis produced five MMIT clusters, spanning municipalities nearing elimination to areas with sustained high local transmission and distinct profiles of declining transmission with intense vs. moderate importation. Overall, 959,281 cases (17.38%) were imported. Cases were predominantly Pv (81.68%), with Pf comprising 17.15%; Pf was more common among imported than locally acquired infections. Mobility patterns shifted after mid-2020: by 2023, > 50% of exported cases originated in mining localities despite ~0.2% land coverage, with Pf importation increasingly concentrated in municipalities overlapping the Yanomami Indigenous Land. From 2006–2023, we identified 63 Pf and 221 Pv reintroduced locally acquired cases following ≥3 years of zero local transmission, leading to reestablishment in 6 and 23 municipalities, respectively, and generating 864 subsequent Pf and 6,524 subsequent Pv cases. Post-reintroduction transmission persisted for long periods (mean 762 days for Pf; 815 days for Pv).

Conclusion

Malaria elimination in Brazil is increasingly hindered by parasite-specific mobility, especially linked to mining–indigenous confluences, and by repeated reintroduction in receptive municipalities nearing elimination (notably along the arc of deforestation). Mobility-informed surveillance and targeted reactive strategies are essential to achieve and sustain Brazil’s malaria elimination goals.

title: HiFIseek: Gene-specific enrichment of high-impact mutations in associated genomic regions
content:
by Rafael Riudavets Puig, Denise G. O’Mahony, Ina Skaara Brorson, Ksenia Sokolova, Vessela N. Kristensen, Anthony Mathelier

Transcription is regulated through the sequence-specific binding of transcription factors (TFs) to cis-regulatory regions (CRRs); DNA variants in CRRs can disrupt TF-DNA interactions and gene regulatory networks through a cascading effect. Despite a few cases of reported recurrent cis-regulatory variants (CRVs), another approach for detecting non-coding functional events rely on combining gene-CRR associations capturing the regulatory elements controlling gene transcription, and functional impact (FI) scores quantifying the deleterious effect of variants. While many methods exist for each, how much they agree and how strongly the choice of CRR-FI score combination impacts the prediction of cis-regulatory altered genes has not been systematically assessed. Here, we demonstrate that gene-CRR associations and FI scoring methods exhibit little consensus, highlighting the impact of the choice of a specific CRR-FI score combination in a given analysis. These observations point to the need for a systematic approach to evaluate several gene-CRR and FI scoring methods in a unified framework. To address this gap, we developed HiFIseek, a Snakemake pipeline of two enrichment detection methods exploring the enrichment of high FI variants in CRRs associated with a gene using all region-score combinations. We applied HiFIseek to detect genes exhibiting high functional impact CRVs in eight cancer cohorts and a set of breast cancer risk-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). We demonstrate that cancer driver genes exhibit a higher frequency of FI CRVs compared to non-cancer genes. In the cancer cohorts, HiFIseek detected genes pointing to cancer-related pathways with enrichment for high FI CRVs despite a small degree of agreement across CRR-FI score combinations. In the SNP cohort, HiFIseek found again small consensus across CRR-score combinations, one of which returned 18 known cancer-related genes, including BRCA1, showing an enrichment of high-impact CRVs.

title: CardamomOT: A mechanistic optimal transport-based framework for gene regulatory network inference, trajectory reconstruction and generative modeling
content:
by Yann Maugé, Elias Ventre

A key challenge in inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) governing cellular processes such as differentiation and reprogramming from experimental data lies in the impossibility of directly measuring protein dynamics at the single-cell level, which prevents establishing causal relationships between regulator activity and target responses. In earlier work, we introduced CARDAMOM, an algorithm that uses temporal snapshots of scRNA-seq data to calibrate a GRN-driven mechanistic model of gene expression. However, this method had several limitations: it could only rely on the relative ordering of time points rather than their exact labels, imposed restrictive quasi-stationary assumptions on protein dynamics, and depended on multiple hyperparameters. Here, we present CardamomOT, a new method based on the same mechanistic model that jointly reconstructs the GRN and unobserved protein trajectories from the data within a mechanistic optimal transport framework. By incorporating exact time labels and priors on protein kinetic rates from the literature, and substantially reducing the number of required hyperparameters, our approach addresses these limitations and substantially improves the accuracy and robustness of GRN calibration. We validate our framework on both in silico and experimental datasets, demonstrating computational scalability and consistently improved performance over state-of-the-art methods in both GRN and trajectory reconstruction on simulated datasets, and, on experimental datasets, reconstruction of cellular trajectories, velocity fields and latent protein levels that are mutually consistent, together with GRN structures consistent with known biology. We also show that these improvements make the calibrated mechanistic model suitable to be used as a generative model to generate testable predictions of cellular responses to unseen perturbations. To our knowledge, this is among the first methods to explicitly integrate mechanistic GRN inference, trajectory reconstruction, and simulation of realistic datasets into a unified framework for scRNA-seq time series analysis.

title: Omics data discovery agents: Agent-supported retrieval, reanalysis, and synthesis of published omics data
content:
by Alexandre Hutton, Jesse G. Meyer

The biomedical literature contains a vast collection of omics studies, yet most published data remain functionally inaccessible for computational reuse. When raw data are deposited in public repositories, essential information for reproducing reported results is dispersed across main text, supplementary files, and code repositories, and in the rarer cases where intermediate data (e.g., protein abundance files) are shared, their location is irregular. Here we present an agentic framework for the agent-supported retrieval, reanalysis, and synthesis of published omics data. The system employs large language model (LLM) agents with access to tools for fetching omics studies, extracting article metadata, identifying and downloading published data, executing containerized quantification pipelines, and synthesizing results across studies. Applied at corpus scale, the pipeline catalogued dataset references across thousands of PubMed Central articles; we report these as descriptive system outputs rather than as a validated measure of extraction accuracy. Using model context protocol (MCP) servers to expose containerized analysis tools, the agents retrieved and re-quantified data in five end-to-end reanalyses spanning data-dependent and data-independent proteomics and bulk RNA-seq. All five reanalyses completed, each with documented human guidance and workflow accommodations, and reproduced the authors’ deposited abundances with high per-sample correlation (0.85–0.997) and strongly concordant differentially expressed features (fold-change Spearman 0.88–0.91), with no direction reversals among features called differentially expressed in both analyses; residual differences in significant-feature lists were attributable to threshold placement, tool-version, and preprocessing differences rather than to the underlying quantities. We further demonstrate that agents can identify semantically similar studies, judge data compatibility, and synthesize findings across studies, including a random-effects meta-analysis that recovered consistent protein regulation in liver fibrosis. Rather than a validated benchmark of literature-wide performance, this work is a feasibility demonstration together with an auditable, reusable toolset, establishing a foundation for prospective evaluation of automated omics-data reuse.

title: A binding-activated CRISPR/dCas13X imaging system enables precise RNA tracking in plants
content:
by Jiayu Zhang, Yiran Tao, Yun Zhao, Miaomiao Lei, Yucheng Shen, Qicong Li, Chenxu Liu, Jiuyuan Bai

Visualizing the spatiotemporal dynamics of native RNA molecules with single-transcript-level sensitivity in living plant cells remains a formidable challenge due to the high background noise caused by the unique cellular architecture of plants. Here, using transiently transformed Nicotiana benthamiana cells and stable Arabidopsis thaliana lines, we present a high-signal-to-noise RNA imaging platform that couples CRISPR–dCas13X with a binding-associated fluorescence stabilization strategy. We identified a novel plant-specific degron that selectively targets unbound probes for proteasomal degradation while preserving target-associated signal in a manner consistent with binding-dependent protection, enabling high-fidelity detection of endogenous mRNA puncta with minimal perturbation. Leveraging this platform, we characterized dynamics of FT mRNA trafficking in living plant cells, including plasmodesmata-targeting, cell-to-cell trafficking, and long-distance movement. Loss-of-function analysis further identified the established RNA-binding protein GRP7 as a factor that contributes to efficient FT mRNA transport. This work establishes a useful toolkit for investigating plant RNA biology and provides mechanistic insight into the systemic transport of florigenic signals.

title: Inadequate antibody validation places substantial numbers of animal and human tissue samples at risk of waste
content:
by Michael Biddle, Jemma Cooper, Katherine Blades, Dominic Ruddy, Eva M. Krockow, Harvinder Virk

Lack of antibody validation by researchers frequently misdirects biomedical research, yet the ethical consequences—particularly avoidable use of animal and human biological materials—remain unquantified. Using focus groups (n = 12), surveys (n = 107), and systematic analysis of 785 publications, we examined how researchers select and validate antibodies, and quantified the downstream ethical costs. Antibody selection is substantially influenced by social factors such as previous laboratory use and peer recommendations, while systematic evaluation of performance characteristics remains limited. From a dataset of 614 antibodies subjected to rigorous characterisation using knockout controls, 97 (15.8%) failed across all tested applications; we systematically searched for publications linked to these antibodies. Within the 760 publications (those where validation status could be confirmed), only 120 (15.8%) presented any validation evidence—despite 72.0% of surveyed researchers reporting having used at least one recommended validation method. The remaining 640 papers reported a minimum of 8,064 animal samples and 4,424 human tissue samples used with antibodies of demonstrated poor performance and without evidence of fitness for the specific experimental purpose; we describe these as samples at risk of waste. Reserving the term waste for samples used with reagents since withdrawn from sale, and therefore irreproducible, conservative extrapolation gives lower-bound, order-of-magnitude estimates of millions of animal and human tissue samples consumed globally. Researchers identified time, cost, and lack of supervisor support as primary barriers, whilst strongly supporting open data sharing, dedicated validation funding, and publisher requirements as solutions. These findings provide a first quantification of the ethical costs of inadequate antibody validation and highlight the need for coordinated stakeholder interventions to reduce avoidable biological sample waste in biomedical research.

title: Actionable solutions to address antibody validation failures
content:
by Katherine Blades, Michael Biddle, Robert Froud, Eva M. Krockow, Harvinder Virk

The experimental use of antibodies that have not been validated for context-specific use frequently misdirects biomedical research. Experimental results that derive from the use of inadequately validated antibodies are estimated to waste over $1 billion annually in the United States alone and to consume millions of animal and human biological samples in experiments whose conclusions may be unreliable. Community validation frameworks, reporting standards, and independent characterisation initiatives have made important progress, and multi-stakeholder coordination efforts are emerging. However, the research community lacks a formally developed, consensus-based action plan that specifies what each stakeholder group should do, by when, and with what priority. We conducted a modified Delphi study with international experts representing academic researchers, scientific publishers, research funders, antibody manufacturers, and institutional research leaders to develop actionable recommendations for improving antibody validation, selection, and reporting practices. Thirty-two participants rated 33 proposed actions on effectiveness and feasibility using 9-point scales, with consensus assessed using the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method. Over two rounds, the panel achieved consensus on 15 items as both effective and feasible for implementation by 2030. These spanned institutional actions (training in antibody validation, integration into research integrity frameworks, support for local expertise networks), funder actions (dedicated validation budgets, grant application requirements, endorsement of community reporting standards), publisher actions (complete antibody reporting packages, clear validation standards), manufacturer actions (assignment of unique identifiers at source), and cross-stakeholder coordination (a shared roadmap for improvement). An additional 15 items were rated as effective but with uncertain feasibility, reflecting a consistent pattern in which the panel agreed on the value of proposed interventions but expressed reservations about realistic implementation timelines. One item was rejected by the panel with concerns around effectiveness and feasibility. Participants described four interconnected barriers to progress: diffuse ownership of the problem across stakeholders; market dynamics that inadequately reward antibody quality; difficulty justifying investment when returns are distributed across the research system; and coordination challenges among actors with different incentive structures. These barriers are addressable through coordinated action, and the findings complement existing technical and data-sharing initiatives by providing the structured, expert-informed policy framework to help translate awareness of the problem into concrete practice and policy changes.

title: Rethinking ocean alkalinity enhancement
content:
Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, Published online: 06 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43017-026-00828-5

Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) is often thought of as a global-scale geoengineering approach to mitigate climate change. This Perspective explores the environmental effects, geochemical constraints, verification and governance of OAE and argues for local-scale, context-led evaluation.
