title: Interdecadal Phase Shifts of Winter Asian‐Pacific Oscillation Modulate the Warm Arctic‐Cold Eurasia Pattern
content:
Abstract
Against the backdrop of global warming, warm Arctic‐cold Eurasia (WACE) has garnered extensive scientific attention. However, the drivers of its interdecadal variability remain insufficiently understood. Using reanalysis data and pre‐industrial control simulations, we demonstrate that winter Asian‐Pacific Oscillation (APO), a dominant upper‐tropospheric atmospheric mode over the Asian‐North Pacific sector, modulates the WACE variability at the interdecadal timescale. Positive APO phases tend to induce anomalous warming over the Barents‐Kara Seas (BKS) and cooling over central Asia. Information flow and Granger causality diagnostics confirm the causal effect of APO on the WACE. Physically, positive APO phases feature upper‐tropospheric warming and anticyclonic circulation anomalies over Asia, which are accompanied by cyclonic circulation anomalies over central Asia that favor local cooling. Reduced background potential vorticity gradient over the Ural‐Siberian region further facilitates persistent high‐pressure anomalies near the BKS, ultimately resulting in anomalous warming in situ.

title: Corals Reveal Atlantic Drivers of Red Sea Surface Variability Through Indian Ocean Inflow
content:
Abstract
Sea surface temperature (SST) and salinity (SSS) variability in the Red Sea influences marine ecosystems, hydrologic variability, and circulation within and outside of the Red Sea. However, understanding of multidecadal surface variability in the Red Sea is limited by short and sparse observational records. To extend beyond the limited observational period, we present 346 years of paired records of Sr/Ca and δ18O from a central Red Sea Porites sp. coral providing centuries‐long, sub‐annually resolved records of SST and relative SSS (δ18Osw) variability. We synthesize our records with published northern Red Sea coral records to investigate basin‐scale patterns. Both sites exhibit coherent multidecadal SST and δ18Osw variability, which are anticorrelated to the Atlantic Multidecadal Variability and document the crucial role of Indian Ocean inflow in modulating Red Sea surface conditions. Our results refine our understanding of multidecadal drivers of Red Sea surface conditions, with implications for regional hydrology, circulation, and ecology.

title: Drift‐Resonance Driven by Field Line Resonance Gradients: A Mechanism for Non‐Dispersive Microinjection Events
content:
Abstract
Ultra‐low‐frequency waves in the magnetosphere often produce field line resonances with strong spatial gradients in wave amplitude. We analyze a form of drift resonance driven by these gradients near the resonant field line. This mechanism differs fundamentally from conventional gradient‐ and curvature‐driven drift resonance and predicts an energy‐independent, non‐dispersive signature in particle flux. Observations from the Magnetospheric Multiscale mission reveal a non‐dispersive electron microinjection event occurring near the resonant L‐shell of a toroidal wave, providing the first direct evidence for this resonance type in the terrestrial magnetosphere. We present a classification of particle‐wave interactions that includes both trapped and passing drift‐resonant populations, demonstrating how field line resonance structures can generate rapid, coherent microinjections distinct from classical drift‐resonance behavior.

title: High‐ and Low‐Latitude Insolation Forcing Drives the Half‐Precession Cycle in Winter Arctic Sea Ice
content:
Abstract
The half‐precession cycle is a key climatic signal in global climate system, linking high‐ and low‐latitude climate variability and bridging orbital‐ and millennial‐scale climate changes. While it characterizes tropical insolation, its origin in high‐latitude climate records remains unclear. Based on a transient climate simulation spanning the past 800,000 years, here we find that in response to astronomical forcing, the eccentricity‐modulated half‐precession cycle emerges as an evident signal in the winter Arctic sea ice variability. It is driven by the combined influence of summer insolation at northern high latitudes and winter northward atmospheric heat transport, with the latter being primarily regulated by winter insolation at low latitudes. Moreover, the half‐precession cycle in winter Arctic sea ice leaves a distinct imprint on Arctic Ocean surface albedo as well as upward heat and moisture fluxes, which may serve as an important mechanism to explain the half‐precession signal observed in high latitudes.

title: Physical controls dominate stream metabolism and carbon cycling over nutrients and stoichiometry
content:
Abstract
Streams process and transport vast carbon quantities along the aquatic continuum. The balance between processing and downstream export is governed by metabolism, which in turn is regulated by distinct physicochemical controls that vary through space and time. However, macronutrient stoichiometry is rarely considered over absolute concentrations. Here, we examined physical, chemical, and stoichiometric controls on stream metabolism, organic carbon mineralization, and carbon spiraling over 2 years. Stream discharge, temperature, and light were the primary drivers across metabolic and carbon cycling parameters. In generalized additive models, physical variables accounted for up to four times more deviance than stoichiometry, with consistently more important associations in partial least squares regressions. Increased discharge and temperature promoted heterotrophy and strongly controlled metabolic balance, while dissolved C : P and C : N provided minor moderating effects. Our study highlights varied physical controls on stream metabolic processes and suggests nutrient concentrations and stoichiometry are secondary regulators, especially when C : N : P are non‐limiting—an important reflection when evaluating future effects of nutrient pollution on the global carbon cycle.

title: Nonlinear dynamics of time-variable slope circulation
content:
Nonlinear dynamics of time-variable slope circulation
Anna Lina Petruseviciute Sjur, Pål Erik Isachsen, Johan Nilsson, and Susan Elizabeth Allen
Ocean Sci., 22, 3055–3078, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3055-2026, 2026
Ocean currents along continental slopes do not respond linearly to changing winds. Nonlinearities arises from interactions between the flow and seafloor bumps. Using simplified simulations and theory, we investigate the dynamics of these nonlinear effects. Such effects are likely missed in coarse-grained climate models, with implications for representing ocean flow in areas such as the Arctic.

title: Storm-modulated submesoscale dynamics over sloping topography in a wind-driven, non-tidal basin
content:
Storm-modulated submesoscale dynamics over sloping topography in a wind-driven, non-tidal basin
Evridiki Chrysagi, Lars Umlauf, Ulf Gräwe, Hans Burchard, and Alberto C. Naveira Garabato
Ocean Sci., 22, 3037–3053, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3037-2026, 2026
High-resolution numerical simulations of the Baltic Sea reveal that fine-scale features known as submesoscales are widespread in the deeper layers of the basin, especially near its boundaries. These features are linked to strong mixing and, in this wind-driven system, are found to intensify during storms, with wind reversals shifting the location of mixing hotspots. Our results suggest that storm-modulated submesoscales may be important in other wind-driven coastal seas and lakes.

title: The Gαi/o GPCR LPAR2 Acts as a Non-Classical Factor for Aldosterone Induced Injury in a Cardiomyocyte Model
content: Aldosterone is a key regulator of systemic sodium, potassium, and fluid homeostasis. Chronic elevation of aldosterone, as observed in primary aldosteronism, chronic heart and kidney diseases, promotes cardiac hypertrophy, inflammation, fibrosis, and heart failure, which are further enhanced in aging. Although these pathological effects are primarily attributed to the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR), emerging evidence suggests roles for nonclassical G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling. We identified lysophosphatidic acid receptor 2 (LPAR2) as a novel GPCR candidate that mediates aldosterone signaling in cardiomyocytes. Using AC16 human cardiomyocyte cells and reporter gene assays, we demonstrate that aldosterone activates a Gi/o-dependent GPCR pathway. Pharmacological inhibition of LPAR2 internalization confirms its specific reaction to aldosterone. Functional studies revealed that aldosterone-induced cardiomyocyte injury requires both MR and LPAR2, where specific antagonists to both receptors reduced the ability of aldosterone to induce collagen expression and cell death markers. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized non-classical mechanism of aldosterone action in the heart and highlight LPAR2 as a promising therapeutic target for aldosterone-driven cardiovascular disease.

title: Monitoring the translation initiation process in prokaryotes via large-scale examination using optimized SSU-seq technique
content: Translation initiation is a critical stage of protein synthesis in prokaryotes, where ribosomes assemble on mRNA to begin decoding genetic information. The interactions between ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and mRNA significantly influence this process, with features like ribosomal binding site (RBS) affecting ribosomal dynamics. However, direct experimental validation of these types of interaction is yet to be provided. In this study, we developed an optimized small sub-unit sequencing (SSU-seq) protocol for Escherichia coli, enabling the detailed examination of ribosomal complexes and subunits dynamics. Unlike Ribo-seq, which primarily maps fully assembled ribosomes, SSU-seq captures both ribosomal subunits and intact ribosomes, offering a comprehensive view of translation initiation and elongation events. By integrating experimental data with predictive models, our study advances the understanding of translation regulation in prokaryotes and underscores the utility of SSU-seq in decoding the complexities of ribosome-mRNA interactions. Our analysis reveals distinct patterns of small subunit distribution across the entire mRNAs with higher density near positions with stronger rRNA-mRNA hybridization. The results may suggest that rRNA-mRNA hybridization positions along the entire transcript facilitate efficient start codon recognition by maintaining proximity between the small subunit and the mRNA.

title: Impact of oxygen fluctuation and consumption on the dynamics of a reduced go-or-grow model for tumor cell invasion
content: We propose a minimal mathematical framework to describe the go-or-grow dynamics of tumor cells comprising two phenotypically distinct populations. One population is migratory and undergoes constant diffusion, while the other proliferates in an oxygen-dependent manner. The local oxygen concentration governs transitions between these phenotypes. We then ask whether the time scale of cyclic hypoxia, where oxygen is spatially homogeneous but fluctuates between normoxic and hypoxic levels over time, alters the dynamics of the reduced generalist model in the fast phenotype-switching regime compared with the full go-or-grow model. We observe that the reduced generalist phenotype model fails to capture the go-or-grow dynamics under rapid oxygen fluctuations. Our results predict that the tumor growth rate increases in the generalist-phenotype model under rapid oxygen fluctuations compared with tumors of the proposed go-or-grow model. We then explore whether oxygen consumption, which leads to spatial heterogeneity in oxygen concentration, plays a role in distinguishing the dynamics of the reduced model from the proposed go-or-grow model. We demonstrate that the tumor in the proposed go-or-grow model exhibits a higher growth rate than the tumor in the reduced generalist-phenotype model under a slow oxygen consumption rate.

title: RI-SINDy: Regulation-Informed Sparse Model Discovery in Biological Gene Networks
content: Oscillatory and saturating dynamics in regulatory gene networks govern processes such as cell cycle timing, circadian rhythms, and inflammatory signaling, and sparse regression methods such as SINDy offer an interpretable method for recovering their governing equations from time-series data. However, these networks are typically governed by Hill-type nonlinearities that become nearly collinear with polynomial candidates over most bounds of an oscillating curve, and placing them in a shared library produces ill-conditioned regressions and unreliable coefficient estimates. Standard approaches such as ridge regularization, library normalization, and orthogonalization can marginally improve conditioning but cannot remove the structural multicollinearity of these systems, in turn limiting our ability to produce accurate parameter estimates. To address this issue, we propose the Regulation-Informed Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (RI-SINDy) method, which removes known regulatory terms from the regression and recovers their coefficients directly from an asymptotic drift-balance condition. Because the time averaged derivative of a bounded trajectory approaches zero, the coefficients of regulatory nonlinearities can be computed independently by constraining them to offset the mean contribution of the remaining terms. We demonstrate that this method effectively reduces library collinearity and improves conditioning numbers by 3-45x, substantially improving coefficient recovery and regression accuracy. We test the RI-SINDy method on experimental Hes1 data and on synthetic Goodwin and NF-{kappa}B models. On Hes1, it achieves the lowest trajectory error among the compared methods (Traditional SINDy, SR3, and Nullcline Reconstruction). On the synthetic systems, it recovers the correct sparse structure with lower trajectory error than SR3 and Nullcline Reconstruction, and in a Goodwin noise sweep it recovers all active terms at noise levels up to 15%, where Traditional SINDy and E-SINDy fail to. In conclusion, the RI-SINDy method provides a robust framework to overcome the issue of multicollinearity for system identification in biological systems.

title: Gain of Function Cytolysin Variant Expressed by Clinically Isolated Urinary Enterococcus faecalis
content: Cytolysin is a toxin-bacteriocin commonly encoded by Enterococcus faecalis that can target erythrocytes, neutrophils, and macrophages as well as other Gram-positive bacteria. Cytolysin can lyse human, horse, rabbit, and mouse erythrocytes, but not sheep erythrocytes (SEs). It is hypothesized that SEs are resistant to cytolysin because they lack phosphatidylcholine (PC) in their membranes, while susceptible erythrocytes have PC-rich membranes, suggesting PC as a cytolysin binding target. Here, we isolated a urinary E. faecalis strain C33 that can efficiently lyse SEs and found that this activity was conserved among several E. faecalis clinical isolates. We demonstrated that although C33 cytolysin was necessary for SE lysis, it was not sufficient, suggesting a secondary factor enhances cytolysin activity against SEs. Through liposome assays we found that while PC was required for the activity of DS16 cytolysin, PC was dispensable for C33 cytolysin activity. To assess the biological significance of C33 cytolysin in the bladder microenvironment, we assessed C33 cytolysin activity against bladder epithelial cells and the urinary microbiota. We found that C33 cytolysin was more cytotoxic to human bladder epithelial cells than the canonical DS16 cytolysin. We also found greater inhibition of co-isolated urinary microbiota species Streptococcus parasanguinis, Enterococcus raffinosus, Staphylococcus capitis, and Corynebacterium coyleae by C33 cytolysin. Interestingly, E. faecalis C33 also inhibited the protective urogenital taxa Lactobacillus crispatus and Bifidobacterium longum. Together, these results reveal a new PC-independent cytolysin activity among clinical E. faecalis isolates that may support survival and competition in the urinary microenvironment.

title: CorB and MgpB (YegH) alleviate excess-magnesium stress and contribute to egg white tolerance and virulence in Salmonella
content: Maintaining proper cation homeostasis is essential for the survival of all living organisms. During infection, Salmonella must adapt to host-imposed magnesium (Mg2+) limitation. To compensate, Salmonella induces high-affinity Mg2+ transporters and synthesis of polyamines, organic cations that partially substitute for Mg2+. Once Mg2+ levels are restored and cells enter stationary phase, excess cations must be exported; failure to do so results in loss of viability. The CorC-domain protein PaeA exports excess polyamines, whereas MgpA and CorC reduce intracellular Mg2+ levels. Here, we identify two new CorC-domain proteins, MgpB (formerly YegH) and CorB, as mediators of Mg2+ homeostasis, showing that they also reduce intracellular Mg2+ accumulation and protect cells from endogenous excess-cation stress. Genetic analyses revealed the functional redundancy among these proteins in conferring resistance to exogenous high Mg2+, endogenous stress induced after Mg2+ starvation, and egg whites. Deletion of mgpB and/or corB conferred little to no phenotype. However, these mutations showed synergistic phenotypes in strains lacking MgpA. This synergistic relationship was also evident in mouse competition assays. Lack of MgpA, CorC, MgpB, and CorB leads to an increase in intracellular Mg2+ levels. Moreover, expression of mgpB and corB are increased in high Mg2+, all consistent with their role as putative Mg2+ exporters. Together, these findings identify MgpB and CorB as new mediators of Mg2+ homeostasis and reveal a multilayered system that enables Salmonella to finely balance intracellular cation levels during environmental and host-imposed stress.

title: A TLR2-associated entry pathway promotes productive dengue virus serotype 2 infection and inflammatory responses in classical monocytes
content: Severe dengue is characterized by systemic inflammation and vascular leakage. Recent evidence indicates that Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) supports early steps of dengue virus (DENV) infection in monocytes, whereas intracellular viral RNA sensing drives much of the subsequent inflammatory response. However, whether this entry-associated function of TLR2 differs among human monocyte subsets remains unknown. Here, we investigated how the TLR2 axis regulates DENV serotype 2 (DENV2) infection and inflammatory output in purified primary human monocytes and sorted monocyte subsets. Blocking TLR2 at the cell surface or targeting its intracellular TIR domain reduced virus-cell association, productive infection, and the release of inflammatory and antiviral mediators. Among TLR2-associated receptors, CD14 and, to a lesser extent, CD36 contributed to efficient infection, whereas TLR1, TLR6, and TLR10 were dispensable under the conditions tested. Notably, TLR2 blockade reduced viral production and cytokine release in CD16- classical monocytes but not in pooled CD16+ monocytes, identifying a subset-specific dependence on the TLR2 axis. TLR3 contributed to inflammatory and antiviral responses without affecting viral replication, consistent with post-entry recognition of viral RNA. Finally, blocking the TLR2 axis during monocyte infection prevented the loss of endothelial barrier integrity induced by monocyte-derived soluble mediators. Together, these findings identify a TLR2-associated entry route that preferentially supports productive DENV2 infection in classical monocytes and thereby enables RNA-sensor-dependent inflammatory responses that compromise endothelial function.

title: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications control the antiviral response to influenza A virus infection by limiting IFITM2/3 expression
content: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications regulate diverse cellular processes, including the response to virus infection. However, how m6A controls antiviral gene expression and whether effects on viral replication are due to direct modification of viral RNA or regulation of cellular transcripts remain unclear. Herein, we analysed how m6A modifications control the cell-autonomous innate immune response to influenza A virus (IAV) infection. Depletion or inhibition of the m6A writer METTL3 or the m6A reader YTHDF2 restricts IAV replication. However, using a quantitative method to identify m6A sites, we did not detect substantial m6A modification of viral RNA. In contrast, many IAV-induced cellular transcripts were m6A modified in their coding region, including those that encode pattern recognition receptors and direct antiviral proteins. Inhibition of interferon signalling restored IAV replication after METTL3 inhibition, highlighting that m6A controls the antiviral response to infection. METTL3 inhibition increased expression of the paralogous antiviral proteins IFITM2 and IFITM3, which were required for the antiviral activity of the METTL3 inhibitor. We propose that m6A modifications regulate the expression of antiviral proteins to limit the magnitude of their induction and balance antiviral activity with maintaining cellular homeostasis.

title: The polysaccharide portion of LPS is critical for caspase-11 inflammasome activation
content: Caspase-11 (Casp11) is a murine zymogen that becomes active upon sensing cytosolic lipopolysaccharide (LPS), enabling it to form the non-canonical inflammasome and execute an inflammatory cell death known as pyroptosis. The lipid A acylation state of LPS is thought to be the primary regulator of Casp11 activation. However, our data demonstrate that the polysaccharide moiety of LPS, and particularly the polysaccharide phosphates, are critical for eliciting maximal Casp11 activation. Accordingly, the polysaccharide was required for Rhodobacter sphaeroides LPS to act as an inflammasome antagonist. Furthermore, isolated polysaccharide was sufficient to antagonize Casp11 activation. Mechanistically, our findings support a two-step model of non-canonical inflammasome activation where the polysaccharide recruits Casp11 to LPS and the lipid A acylation state governs oligomerization efficiency. These findings provide new insight into the molecular basis of LPS-driven Casp11 activation, with implications for the design of future therapies that target the non-canonical inflammasome.

title: Contact-dependent growth inhibition drives kin discrimination and shapes in vivo strain dominance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection
content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a ubiquitous environmental bacterium and an opportunistic pathogen. Rather than existing as single clonal lineages, environmental and clinical populations often consist of a mixture of distinct strains that directly compete to dominate the niche. To eliminate rivals, P. aeruginosa deploys a form of interference competition termed contact-dependent growth inhibition (CDI). CDI is mediated by CdiA, where, upon cell contact, the CdiA C-terminal toxin domain is delivered to prey cells. Toxin-producing cells encode for a cognate CdiI immunity protein to prevent self-intoxication. Different strains of P. aeruginosa encode for CdiA proteins with different C-terminal toxin domains and cognate CdiI immunity proteins. Most studies have relied on engineered strains to investigate the mechanism of CDI. While extremely useful for studying CdiA-mediated intoxication, such work masks the true diversity of wild-type CdiA variants and their impact on competitive interactions between strains. In this study, we systematically investigated CDI-mediated competition using unique conspecific strains of P. aeruginosa. We identified several novel CdiA toxin domains and mapped the competitive outcomes they govern. Furthermore, using a mouse model of acute pneumonia, we demonstrate that CDI-mediated interference competition actively occurs during mixed-strain infections in vivo. Together, our findings reveal that P. aeruginosa leverages CDI as a potent, strain-dependent kin discrimination mechanism that directly shapes population dynamics and strain dominance within host and natural environments.

title: Positive control of the integrative and conjugative element Tn916 and its limited gene expression in transconjugants
content: Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) are widespread in bacteria and typically confer important phenotypes to their hosts. Following excision from the host chromosome, an ICE can transfer to a new cell through the element-encoded conjugation machinery (a type IV secretion system) to create a transconjugant. Tn916, a well-studied ICE that confers tetracycline resistance, is found in several Gram-positive pathogens and has been widely studied in Bacillus subtilis. Unlike most ICEs, Tn916 causes host-cell death following its activation (excision and gene expression). We found that orf7 and orf8 (renamed sig7 and sig8), two regulatory genes in Tn916, encode a two-subunit (split) sigma factor of RNA polymerase, Sig7-8, that activates transcription from Porf7 (now Psig7) and is required for excision of the element. Importantly, production of Sig7-8, either from Psig7 or another strong promoter, caused cell death. Using a Cre recombinase reporter to detect gene expression, we detected little or no transcription from Psig7 in transconjugants. This lack of transcription from Psig7 in transconjugants was essential for fitness of both the element and its host: forcing transcription from Psig7 in transconjugants caused either loss of Tn916 or death of nascent transconjugants. Our findings indicate that, unlike other well-studied ICEs (e.g., ICEBs1) that use repressors to control gene expression and are expressed in nascent transconjugants, most Tn916 genes remain off following transfer to a new host. This regulation prevents Tn916 from killing transconjugants and allows successful horizontal transfer and maintains the potential for future activation in the new host.

title: Thermodynamically controlled biokinetics modelling of a lindane-degrading anaerobic enrichment culture
content: The anaerobic biotransformation of lindane ({gamma}-hexachlorocyclohexane), a persistent legacy pesticide and challenging subsurface contaminant was modelled using an integrated Monod biokinetics framework. Calibrated against batch experimental data, this model accounted for the dissolution of solid phase lindane and the thermodynamics of reactions involved. The study focused on a methanogenic, lindane-degrading enrichment culture (GT2) that used ethanol as the electron donor, where ethanol fermentation supplied hydrogen to support reductive dechlorination of lindane. A Dehalobacter strain was identified as the lindane-degrading organism, while a member of bacterial order Geobacterales carried out ethanol fermentation. First-order decay constants for lindane-degrading Dehalobacter were estimated from experimental data and showed variation across different growth conditions. The biokinetics model captured interactions among key microbial processes, namely lindane dechlorination, ethanol fermentation, hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis, and acetoclastic methanogenesis. Thirteen biokinetics parameters including maximum substrate utilization rates (k), half-velocity constants (Ks), and decay constants for these microbial processes were estimated through a Bayesian optimization approach. Global sensitivity analysis showed that eight parameters, primarily k and Ks, had significant linear impact on the model output, whereas responses to decay constants were more variable and potentially non-linear. This study proposed an effective modelling approach for characterizing syntrophic microbial growth within enrichment cultures and provides valuable biokinetics parameters estimates for real-world applications of anaerobic lindane bioremediation.

title: Thermal stress disrupts microbial symbiosis and host activity in the model sponge Ianthella basta
content: Climate change is threatening coral reef ecosystems around the world, causing significant declines in reef organisms, including sponges. The health of sponges is intimately linked to their symbiosis with microorganisms, yet little is known about their integrated response to ocean warming. Here, we present a comprehensive view of the effect of elevated sea surface temperatures (SST) on the model sponge Ianthella basta. I. basta individuals were exposed to temperatures up to 32 {degrees}C, 2-3 {degrees}C above the mean annual maxima. Host gene expression profiles showed an initial response to heat stress after 2 days, and a decreased expression of genes involved in maintaining tissue integrity, pumping capacity, vitamin transport, and stable symbioses after 4 to 8 days. Congruently, heat stressed samples started to show tissue regression and a reduced abundance of the dominant symbionts after 4 days. A significant loss of the symbionts occurred after 8 days, together with a reduction in microbially driven nitrogen cycling and amino-acid transport and an introduction of opportunistic microbes, which could lead to nutrient imbalance and further destabilisation of the holobiont. Together, this work provides important insights into the avenues through which future SST can impact host-microbe interactions in coral reef sponges.

title: Resource-access breadth marks protective strains against toxigenic Clostridioides difficile
content: Antibiotic disruption of gut microbiota creates opportunities for toxigenic Clostridioides difficile. One strategy is to occupy this niche with a non-toxigenic or weakly virulent strain, but even strains that cause little disease may fail to compete during pathogen challenge. We screened 21 sequence type 1 (ST1) isolates for their ability to protect mice co-colonized with toxigenic VPI10463, separating disease potential from protection. Some strains, such as ST1-75, caused little disease and protected, whereas others, such as ST1-68, caused little disease but failed to protect. Metabolomics showed that ST1-75 depleted more proline than ST1-68, whereas another protective strain, ST1-6, had a different metabolic profile; both protective strains nevertheless responded to many substrates. Substrate-utilization profiling revealed that protection across the 21 isolates correlated with amino-acid overlap with VPI10463, but not overall nutrient overlap or shared genome-encoded protein families. Relative amino-acid access explained variation beyond mono-colonization disease potential, and a consumer-resource model showed how nutrient overlap together with additional resource access can support persistence during competition. Additional experiments support that ST1-mediated protection occurs even in the absence of mature B and T cells. These findings distinguish low disease potential from protection, link protection to strain competition, and identify relative resource access as an informative phenotype for prioritizing strains for biotherapeutic testing.

title: Triazole Stress Induces Accelerated Degradation of Aspergillus fumigatus Hmg1
content: Triazole antifungals inhibit the lanosterol C14-demethylase Cyp51A/B and are the first-line treatment for invasive aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. We previously proposed that triazoles impose a secondary constraint on ergosterol biosynthesis through negative feedback regulation of HMG-CoA reductase (Hmg1) through its sterol sensing domain (SSD), and SSD mutations compromise this regulation to produce resistance. The molecular mechanism underpinning this feedback remained unknown. In this study, we show that voriconazole drives accelerated protein degradation of Hmg1 and that SSD mutation abolishes this regulated degradation. Triazole-induced Hmg1 degradation is proteasome-dependent and partially requires the ERAD E3 ubiquitin ligase, HrdA, and INSIG ortholog, InsA, both conserved regulators of HMG-CoA Reductase abundance. We provide genetic evidence that the initiating negative feedback signal is not triazole acting directly on Hmg1 but lanosterol accumulation resulting from Cyp51A/B inhibition. To test whether depleting Hmg1 protein could re-sensitize resistant strains, we utilized a GFP-targeted degradation system designed to target Hmg1 for degradation without engaging its SSD. Combining this system with voriconazole treatment reduced the MIC at least four-fold in both conidia and established hyphae in susceptible and resistant strains. Together, our findings support a model wherein triazole-induced lanosterol accumulation drives HrdA/InsA-dependent accelerated degradation of Hmg1 and establish that pharmacologically inducing this secondary mechanism can enhance triazole activity in both susceptible and resistant isolates.

title: Gut Microbiota Fuel Aging Induced by Mitochondrial Dysfunction
content: Aging is characterized by hallmarks whose mechanistic interdependencies remain poorly defined. Here, we investigate the bi-directional communication between gut microbiota and host mitochondria in the context of immune regulation, healthspan and lifespan. Using a mitochondrial dysfunction PolgAmut mouse model of accelerated aging, we tested the role of mitochondrial dysfunction in modulating microbial homeostasis and aging. We find that impairment of mitochondrial function hastens the decline of microbiota structure over time and induces immune dysregulation and inflammation through metabolic reprogramming of the myeloid immune subset. Further, we find that gut microbiota drives a paradoxical energy state by reducing mitochondrial function systemically while simultaneously driving energy-intensive programs including immune remodelling and protein synthesis, through mTOR signaling. Thus, aging emerges from the progressive imbalance between microbiota-driven energetic demand and declining mitochondrial energy supply. We postulate that microbiota promote host early-life fitness, at the cost of amplifying metabolic stress and inflammation later in life.

title: Particle association and monsoon seasonality influence microbial communities in marine coastal waters of Singapore
content: Marine microbial communities vary seasonally and spatially, shaped by physiochemical gradients and biotic interactions. Spatiotemporal variability of seawater microbiomes in tropical coastal regions is comparatively understudied, especially in Southeast Asia with high pressures from development and anthropogenic activities. Here, we examined the microspatial and temporal variability of bacterioplankton in the Singapore Strait, which is a tropical system in Southeast Asia influenced by monsoons. By applying total community amplicon sequencing to three particle size fractions reflecting microspatial habitats of seawater (0.22-1 {micro}m ''free-living'', 1-10 {micro}m ''large cells and small aggregates'' and 10-150 {micro}m ''particle-associated''), we show that the seawater microbial community was structured by their microspatial habitats, monsoon seasons and physiochemical variables. Monsoon-driven alternation of water masses originating from the South China Sea to the East and from off the Sumatran coast to the West resulted in a distinct community during the Southwest monsoon across all three size fractions. Total DNA (biomass) was lowest in the 10-150 {micro}m fraction, but these particle-associated sequences had the highest diversity and were surprisingly enriched with picocyanobacterial and some pathogenic taxa, potentially reflecting aggregate formation and/or host-derived particle association. This fraction also exhibited greater temporal variability than the two smaller fractions, which could be related to a more heterogenous environment in particle microhabitats. Overall, this study demonstrated compositional variability in the bacterioplankton across space and time in an equatorial region influenced by monsoons.

title: Multi-omic profiling of Plasmodium knowlesi blood stages identifies host adaptation barriers
content: The zoonotic parasite Plasmodium knowlesi has emerged as a widespread cause of human malaria in Southeast Asia. We assembled a high-resolution transcriptome of zoonotic P. knowlesi across its intraerythrocytic developmental cycle and combined transcriptomics, quantitative proteomics and thermal stability measurements to compare parasites cultured in macaque and human red blood cells. We found that P. knowlesi accelerates through the ring stage to settle at the same developmental pace as P. falciparum during the trophozoite and schizont stages. Subsequent multi-omic analysis revealed broad transcriptional and proteomic adaptations of P. knowlesi to the human host cell environment. Parasites cultured in human cells expressed glutathione synthetase earlier and displayed changes in upstream processes that include NADPH production by the pentose phosphate pathway and glutamine synthesis. These changes were accompanied by further differences in the expression of ribosomal subunits and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Together, our findings offer a systems-level view of non-genetic adaptations of P. knowlesi to the human red blood cell environment.

title: Growth, metabolism, and the benefits of clock-enabled anticipation
content: Circadian clocks are found in myriad species across the tree of life. They are commonly assumed to provide a selective advantage by enabling organisms to anticipate daily environmental changes. It has proven remarkably difficult, however, to move beyond this general idea to explain precisely what advantage anticipation confers and to quantify how large this benefit is. Here, we address these challenges by developing a mathematical model of diurnally varying growth and metabolism in the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus, which fixes carbon through photosynthesis during the day and stores a portion of it as glycogen for use during the night. Specifically, we extend the framework introduced by Hwa and coworkers (Scott et al., Science 330, 1099 (2010)), which quantifies the relationship between growth and proteome composition, to a circadian context. We find that the fastest growth is achieved when glycogen production during the day is minimized to the amount required to sustain essential nighttime processes; growth then occurs exclusively during the day, in agreement with experimental observations. However, the slow relaxation of the proteome, arising from the intrinsically slow growth rate of S. elongatus, severely constrains the implementation of this optimal strategy: In the absence of anticipation, the cell must grow at night in order to produce proteins essential for nighttime metabolism. In contrast, with anticipation enabled by a circadian clock, the bacterium can instead adjust its proteome late in the day, allowing it to avoid less efficient nighttime growth altogether, thereby significantly enhancing its growth rate.

title: Structural and Mechanistic Basis of FapB Accessory Functional Amyloid Assembly in Pseudomonas
content: Functional amyloid formation in Pseudomonas biofilms is coordinated by the six-gene Fap operon (fapA-fapF), which governs the production, secretion, and assembly of extracellular fibrils that reinforce the biofilm matrix. FapC, FapB, and FapE constitute the extracellular amyloid. FapC is the major fibrillar component, whereas FapB and FapE occur at lower abundance and other accessory Fap proteins regulate fibril composition, processing, and secretion. We recently determined the structure of FapC, a cross-b-solenoid major Pseudomonas extracellular fibril. The assembly mechanism and architecture of FapB, however, have remained undefined. Here, we elucidate the structural and mechanistic basis of FapB accessory amyloid, from an intrinsically disordered monomer to a cross-b-solenoid fibril. Using well-defined monomeric preparations, controlled fibrillation assays, NMR spectroscopy, cryo-EM, and structure prediction, we show that FapB efficiently self-assembles into structurally homogeneous helical fibrils. FapB fibrillation is highly sensitive to its initial oligomeric state and purity, as well as to environmental factors such as pH. Monomeric FapC does not measurably perturb the disordered conformational ensemble of FapB, whereas preformed FapB and FapC fibrils reciprocally cross-seed each other, revealing direct kinetic coupling between the two amyloid components. Finally, we present a 3.4A resolution cryo-EM structure of the FapB accessory fibril, revealing a compact cross-b-solenoid architecture closely related to that of FapC. Together, these findings establish FapB as an independently amyloidogenic, structurally defined component of the Fap system, provide structural basis for the first of accessory cross-b-solenoid fibril, and reveal a mechanistic framework for the post-secretion assembly of multicomponent extracellular functional amyloids in Pseudomonas biofilms.

title: From Exception to Rule: Widespread Production of Methylated Rhamnolipids in the Burkholderia cepacia Complex
content: Although Burkholderia cenocepacia exhibits biosurfactant-dependent phenotypes and possesses an rhl operon, the chemical identity of its surface-active product has long remained unresolved. The rhl operon of B. cenocepacia harbors an additional gene, rhlM, predicted to encode a methyltransferase, and recently linked to methylated rhamnolipid synthesis in a few Burkholderiaceae. Here, we hypothesized that this biosurfactant remained cryptic due to low expression under standard laboratory conditions. Using a chromosomal Prhl-luxCDABE fusion reporter, we screened diverse nutritional conditions and identified a defined medium containing galactose and urea that strongly induced rhl transcription. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analyses of B. cenocepacia K56-2 extracts identified the biosurfactants as methylated dirhamnolipid congeners, predominantly L-rhamnosyl-L-rhamnosyl-3-hydroxytetradecanoyl-3-hydroxytetradecanoate methyl ester (RR-C14-C14Me). Extending our analysis across the Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) revealed that methylated rhamnolipid production is widespread and restricted to rhl-positive species. Comparative genomic and protein structural analyses further demonstrated high conservation of both the rhlM-containing operon architecture and the RhlM protein across the Bcc. Together, our findings identify the long-standing cryptic biosurfactant of B. cenocepacia as methylated rhamnolipids and establish rhamnolipid methylation as a conserved hallmark across the Bcc, shifting the paradigm of rhamnolipid structural diversity from an isolated exception to a widespread rule.

title: Tracking gene flow in the gut microbiome reveals phage activation and host-range expansion in response to diet
content: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) drives microbial evolution, but what determines when genes move between species within complex communities remains unclear. We developed a junction-resolved metagenomic framework using short-read sequencing to distinguish mobile genetic element activation from de novo transfer and track both longitudinally. In a defined human gut community colonizing mice, mobile element activation was widespread but successful transfer was rare. A prophage carried by invading Phocaeicola vulgatus transferred reproducibly to resident species when the community resisted invasion, but not when dietary perturbation allowed the invader to expand. Transfer required prophage activation and persistence of a permissive recipient and coincided with diversification of a phage receptor-binding protein. Dietary polysaccharides reproduced prophage-associated fitness costs in vitro, and rhamnogalacturonan I induced cell lysis consistent with productive prophage activation. The framework also detected interspecies transfer retrospectively in longitudinal human metagenomes. Thus, diet and community ecology can redirect gene flow through the gut microbiome.

title: Hairpin Architecture and Extended Sequence Context Shape APOBEC3 Mutagenesis in Monkeypox Virus at Different Genomic Scales
content: The 2022 global mpox outbreak was characterized by an unusual accumulation of more than fifty APOBEC-signature substitutions in MPXV genomes. A previous study suggested that these substitutions preferentially occur within and near hairpins or cruciforms - stem-loop structures formed by inverted repeats. Here, we show that this conclusion resulted from an inappropriate statistical analysis and, using two substantially larger datasets, demonstrate that APOBEC-signature mutations are specifically enriched at TC motifs located at the 3' ends of hairpin loops, but not in other regions of hairpins/cruciforms or in their vicinity. We further identified a preference for stem-loop structures with longer stems and shorter loops, consistent with patterns previously reported for the APOBEC mutagenesis in cancer genomes. Our analysis also revealed a positive association between APOBEC-signature mutation propensity and hairpin stability in single-stranded DNA. Nevertheless, stem-loop structures with long stems and short loops are relatively rare in the MPXV genome, limiting their contribution to the genome-wide distribution of APOBEC-signature mutations to a predominantly local effect. In contrast, extended nucleotide context downstream of the TC motif showed strong genome-wide predictive value, with a marked preference for guanine-rich trinucleotide immediately downstream. Analysis of the upstream nucleotide context was consistent with the mutational specificity of APOBEC3A. Together, these results identify distinct structural and sequence determinants of the APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in MPXV and show that local hairpin/cruciform architecture and extended nucleotide context contribute at different genomic scales.

title: Protein-level mapping reveals novel Immune State Types (ISTs) associated with Chlamydia trachomatis infection, inflammatory remodeling, and scarring in trachoma-hyperendemic Amhara Ethiopia
content: ABSTRACT Background: Trachoma remains the leading infectious cause of blindness. Over 100M people are at risk, and 1.9M already live with visual impairment or blindness. Ethiopia bears the greatest burden of disease with ~61M or 59% of the known affected global population. Although Chlamydia trachomatis (Ct) infection initiates disease, infection alone fails to explain why inflammation resolves in some but progresses to irreversible scarring and vision loss in others. Previous studies have largely examined gene expression or limited protein panels, leaving the conjunctival immune protein environment poorly characterized. We hypothesized that distinct conjunctival immune states capture these pathogenic processes and could reveal biomarkers for selecting treatment and surveillance strategies. Methods and Findings: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 667 participants residing in the hyperendemic Amhara region of Ethiopia at least one year after the most recent azithromycin mass drug administration to treat Ct. The upper tarsal conjunctivae was graded for TF and TI, trachomatous inflammation-follicular or intense, respectively; I-TS/TT, inflammation with scarring with or without trichiasis, defined as one or more eyelashes touching the globe of the eye; and TS and TT, scarring with or without trichiasis but no inflammation. T0 represented no trachoma. The protein concentrations of 41 immune mediators were quantified using Meso Scale Discovery electrochemiluminescence immunoassays. Associations with infection and grade were evaluated using covariate-adjusted models with false discovery rate correction. Bernoulli mixture modeling (BMM) revealed four distinct Immune State Types (ISTs). Both approaches supported a shared biological framework characterized by selective immune activation in Ct infection, broad inflammation in TF/TI, and chemokine remodeling versus immune quiescence in the scarred conjunctiva. Ct infection was associated with a focused IFN-{gamma}-centered response. IST1 captured this immune response where 51.9% of the participants had Ct; we therefore termed IST1 Quiescent Infection. In contrast, TF/TI was associated with higher concentrations of proinflammatory, Th1/Th17, chemokine, regulatory, and remodeling pathways mediators. This profile fit well within IST2, termed Broad Inflammation, where 72.4% of the participants had TF/TI. TS/TT retained considerable chemokine activity, whereas I-TS/TT showed a narrower, IL-17A-dominant inflammatory profile. BMM separated scarring into two states characterized by distinct profiles: IST3, Conjunctival Remodeling, with significantly stronger chemokine and T-cell maintenance signals; and IST4, Quiescent Scarring, with the majority of chemokines being significantly downregulated. This suggests that scarred conjunctiva can retain substantial immune activity or shift toward a more attenuated state. Conclusions: This study establishes the first IST framework for trachoma, revealing biologically distinct immune states with different potential clinical implications. IST1 indicates the need for antibiotic treatment, whereas IST2 suggests that novel immunotherapeutics might be effective in thwarting disease progression. The upregulated chemokines in IST3 may indicate risk of progression to TT necessitating prospective studies and potential novel antifibrotic interventions. Together, our findings provide a strong biological foundation for stratifying patients by immune state and matching them to preventive and therapeutic care. Prospective validation and streamlined biomarker panels will support the translation of this framework into field settings to help avert disease progression and blindness.

title: Soil microbiome functions in plant-aphid dynamics are resilient to community restructuring during compost application
content: Abstract Background: Soil microbiomes play critical roles in plant health and resilience, yet it is still poorly understood how disruptions in local microbial communities, such as during soil management, impact these ecological functions. In this study, we investigated how compost addition, a widely used soil management practice, and microbiome origin influence microbiome-mediated plant resistance to insects. We combined surveys of working organic farms across New York with controlled laboratory experiments, amplicon sequencing, plant-insect bioassays, and mass spectrometry. Results: Compost use was associated with shifts in the relative abundance of 20 fungal and 2 bacterial genera across ten working farms. However, no consistent changes in bacterial or fungal diversity or community structure in fields with compost were observed across the farms. Under controlled conditions using a common compost source, compost increased rhizosphere microbial diversity and significantly altered rhizosphere community structure, including the relative abundance of 6 fungal and 41 bacterial genera. Despite these substantial community-level changes, compost did not affect populations of green peach aphids (Myzus persicae) on kale (Brassica oleracea). Instead, aphid populations and plant salicylic acid concentrations were more strongly associated with microbiome origin, demonstrating that compost can substantially restructure soil and rhizosphere microbial communities without corresponding changes in microbiome-mediated plant resistance to insects. Conclusions: Our findings demonstrate that microbial diversity and compositional responses to management are not necessarily reliable indicators of all microbiome functions. More broadly, this work highlights the importance of local soil microbiome variation in shaping plant-insect interactions and emphasizes the need to link community-level responses to direct functional measurements when evaluating microbiome responses to agricultural management.

title: An Expanded Lpt Pathway Couples Surface Lipoprotein Export to Outer Membrane Vesicle Biogenesis in Bacteroides
content: The ecological dominance of Bacteroidota in the human gut microbiota derives from their exceptional capacity to metabolize diverse dietary and host-derived glycans. This ability relies on surface-exposed lipoproteins (SLPs), which are displayed on the bacterial surface and selectively packaged into outer membrane vesicles (OMVs). Although SLP export and OMV biogenesis are tightly coupled, the mechanism linking these processes has remained unknown. Here, we identify LptZ, a previously uncharacterized protein, as a critical link between SLP surface translocation and OMV biogenesis. Cryo-electron tomography of the lptZ mutant revealed chains of vesicles tethered to the outer membrane, offering a rare glimpse into an arrested stage of OMV formation in which vesicle fission is impaired. Proteomic analysis further showed that, in the absence of LptZ, a subset of SLPs fails to reach the cell surface and instead accumulates at the inner membrane. Unexpectedly, LptZ associates with the lipopolysaccharide transport (Lpt) machinery and repurposes it for SLP translocation. Crosslinking experiments revealed selective associations between multiple SLPs and Lpt proteins, providing mechanistic evidence for the direct involvement of the Lpt machinery in SLP trafficking. We further show that the Bacteroides Lpt machinery contains previously unrecognized components, revealing an unanticipated level of specialization relative to canonical Lpt systems. Together, our findings uncover a previously unknown protein export pathway, expand the functional role of the Lpt machinery, and establish a direct mechanistic link between SLP translocation and OMV biogenesis in Bacteroidota.

title: A versatile and stable reporter platform for human rhinovirus and other enteroviruses
content: Human rhinovirus (HRV), a major cause of upper respiratory infections, has increasingly been associated with lower respiratory tract disease. Although tools to investigate HRV pathogenesis are needed, they remain limited. Reporter viruses expressing fluorescent or luminescent proteins are powerful tools for analyzing viral distribution and replication; however, insertion of a reporter gene often impairs viral replication, and the inserted gene is readily lost during serial passage. To address these problems, we established a versatile and stable strategy for generating reporter HRV and other enteroviruses. The gene encoding mScarlet3, a red fluorescent protein, was inserted between the 5'UTR and VP4 gene, a site previously used in other enteroviruses but not in HRV. Optimizing the 2A cleavage sequence between mScarlet3 and VP4 yielded a reporter HRV with growth kinetics comparable to those of the wild-type virus. To improve the genetic stability of the reporter insert, we evaluated GC-content optimization of the reporter gene and relocation of the cis-acting replication element (CRE). GC-content optimization substantially improved reporter stability in both HRV-B14 and EV-A71, whereas CRE relocation provided additional stabilization in EV-A71 but not in HRV-B14, demonstrating the potential applicability of this strategy to other enteroviruses. This strategy for constructing stable reporter HRV and other enteroviruses will facilitate studies of enterovirus pathogenesis.

title: Streptomyces induces unisexual reproduction of a major human fungal pathogen
content: Cryptococcus, a human pathogenic yeast, can undergo unisexual reproduction in the absence of compatible mating partners, yet this developmental program remains poorly understood. Here, we report that tunicamycin, a natural product produced by Streptomyces species, induces a complete unisexual reproductive cycle in different Cryptococcus species. Bacterial confrontation or purified tunicamycin trigger hyphal differentiation, meiotic recombination, and basidiospore formation, as confirmed by whole-genome sequencing and SNP analyses. We further demonstrate that tunicamycin-induced unisexual development requires canonical sexual regulators and meiotic machinery. Transcriptomic profiling reveals staged developmental reprogramming characterized by early induction of stress- and cell cycle-associated genes, followed by enrichment of genes in the filamentation-related pathways. This capacity varies among natural isolates of C. neoformans and was conserved in Cryptococcus gattii. Together, our findings demonstrate that a bacterial metabolite can activate meiotically competent unisexual reproduction, highlighting interkingdom chemical signaling as a potential driver of fungal evolution in natural environments.

title: Killer meiotic driver prevents chromosome loss and enhances fitness in a fungal pathogen
content: Fungal pathogens often carry dispensable chromosomes (DCs) that confer a selective advantage in adverse environments or during host infection but can be spontaneously lost under non-selective conditions. How DCs are maintained in evolving populations remains poorly understood. Here we show that a meiotic driver known as Spore Killer (spok), located on a giant Starship transposon, limits spontaneous loss of a conserved DC in the cross-kingdom pathogen Fusarium oxysporum. Transfer of a functional spok gene, but not of a killing-deficient mutant allele, to a mitotically unstable DC significantly reduced its loss rate, while spok deletion from a stably maintained DC increased loss frequency. Competition experiments between isogenic strains carrying a functional or a killing-deficient spok allele revealed a dramatic fitness gain conferred by Spok killing activity, which required transmission by hyphal fusion. Thus, spoks and their Starship carriers benefit fungal hosts by preventing DC loss and preserving long-term metabolic and pathogenic plasticity.

title: Uncovering novel phage defense systems through genomic island analysis in Streptococcus thermophilus
content: Bacteria encode diverse antiviral defense systems, yet the evolutionary reservoirs that generate this immune innovation remain poorly defined. Although genomic context has been instrumental in discovering defense systems, genomic islands (GIs), variable chromosomal regions enriched in defense genes and proteins of unknown function, have not been systematically explored as sources of new bacterial immunity. Here, using comparative genomics of Streptococcus thermophilus, we identified 30 defense-associated GIs displaying extensive accessory gene diversity. Investigation of candidate loci from three GIs uncovered 15 previously uncharacterized antiviral systems, including 10 with novel architectures or features, revealing the potential within even a small subset of GIs. Several systems were not located near known defense genes, highlighting that GI-based discovery complements the traditional guilt-by-association approach, revealing systems that would otherwise remain undetected. Together, our findings establish GIs as reservoirs of antiviral innovation and provide a framework for uncovering the diversity of bacterial immune systems.

title: Depth-Resolved Microbial Community Structure and Phosphorus Deficiency Across a 34-cm Mat-Sediment Core in Poza Roja 2, Cuatrocienegas
content: Stratified benthic deposits offer crucial modern analogs for Precambrian biogeochemical dynamics, yet whether the vertical organization of deep sedimentary columns reflects depositional history, present-day geochemical conditions, or both remains poorly understood, particularly under extreme oligotrophy. Here, we present a depth-resolved exploratory survey of a continuous 34-cm sediment core partitioned into 11 discrete horizons (L1 to L11) from Poza Roja 2, an alkaline, sub-hypersaline pond in the Cuatro Cienegas Basin, Mexico. Integrating physical stratigraphy, organic carbon and nutrient stoichiometry, and 16S rRNA gene metabarcoding, we evaluated down-core microbial community structure alongside acute phosphorus scarcity. Molar C:Po and N:Po ratios exceeded canonical Redfield proportions (106:16:1) in every layer, by up to 48.5-fold and 87.8-fold, respectively, both peaking in layer L4. Unconstrained ordination (PCoA) and hierarchical clustering grouped the layers into three compositional zones: upper (L2-L4), intermediate (L5-L6), and basal (L8-L11), with L1 and L7 occupying transitional positions. Archaea accounted for 31.0% of prokaryotic reads, ranging from 8.3% (L5) to 43.7% (L9), and were dominated by SM1-50 (Thermoplasmatota) and Halobacteriota. The phototrophic heliobacterium Heliorestis peaked in the intermediate zone (47.6% of bacterial reads in L6). Constrained Redundancy Analysis models lacked statistical significance (P >= 0.12), highlighting the exploratory nature of a single core (n = 11). This pilot characterization provides a baseline for understanding deep biogenic archives under severe nutrient limitation.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis inactivates host oxysterols to impair macrophage cholesterol homeostasis
content: Host oxysterols coordinate macrophage cholesterol homeostasis and antimicrobial defense, but whether pathogens directly target oxysterol signaling is unknown. Here, we identify pathogen-mediated enzymatic oxysterol inactivation as a mechanism by which Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) subverts host cholesterol metabolism. Mtb oxidizes the endogenous oxysterols 27-hydroxycholesterol (27-HC) and 3{beta}-hydroxycholest-5-enoic acid (3{beta}-HCA) into 3-oxo-{Delta}4 metabolites. Sputum lipidomics across TB cohorts on three continents revealed an active-disease signature characterized by 27-HC depletion and accumulation of 27-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one (27-HCO) and 3-oxocholest-4-enoic acid (3O-CA), which normalized with treatment. In infected human macrophages, Mtb 3{beta}-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3{beta}-Hsd) generated 27-HCO. Unlike their parent oxysterols, 27-HCO and 3O-CA did not activate liver X receptor (LXR), and 3O-CA failed to suppress sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2) target genes. Accordingly, 3{beta}-Hsd-deficient Mtb did not induce macrophage cholesterol retention, a phenotype restored by LXR antagonism. Thus, Mtb enzymatically inactivates host oxysterols, disrupting macrophage cholesterol homeostasis and generating treatment-responsive metabolic signatures in human TB.

title: Paired sequencing of IgA-bound bacteria reveals widespread associations between adaptive immunity and gut microbiome gene expression.
content: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody within the mammalian gut, where it binds to both pathogenic and commensal microbes. Despite its prevalence, the impact of IgA upon the biology and behavior of individual microbes remains poorly understood. Here we present Paired Immunoglobulin Sequencing (PIg-seq), a high-throughput method to identify IgA-associated changes in bacterial gene expression. Using PIg-seq we uncover widespread, and in many cases previously unrecognized, transcriptional responses associated with IgA-binding within the mouse gut. While many of these associations are conserved across diverse bacterial lineages, others vary dramatically even between closely related strains, revealing striking strain-level heterogeneity. Most notably, IgA binding is associated with altered expression of bacterial conjugation genes, and multiple prophages, suggesting an exciting link between adaptive immunity and horizontal gene transfer. Together, our findings establish IgA as a key regulator of microbial behavior, with potential consequences for both the ecology and the evolution of the gut microbiome.

title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses
content: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898.

title: Intermediate phenotypic heterogeneity creates an optimal coexistence window in bacteria-phage communities
content: Phenotypic heterogeneity can expand ecological niche space even within a genetically homogeneous population. Recent experiments showed that growth-rate heterogeneity in a clonal bacterial host can stabilize coexistence among multiple phages. Yet this discovery leaves unresolved whether increasing host heterogeneity monotonically promotes coexistence. Here we show that it does not. Using a trait-based bacteria--phage coexistence framework, we find that phage richness is maximized at an intermediate scale of host growth-rate heterogeneity, determined by the match between host phenotypic dispersion and phage niche width. Our results show that optimal phage diversity emerges from an ecological trade-off between two competing effects: increasing phenotypic heterogeneity enables niche differentiation but eventually reduces the host abundance in the preferred niche of each phage. Therefore, our findings predict that experimentally increasing host growth-rate variance at a fixed mean growth rate should produce a nonmonotonic phage richness response, providing a quantitative principle for how intraspecific phenotypic variation shapes biodiversity in microbial ecosystems.

title: Correcting and georeferencing natural history occurrence records with calibrated uncertainty
content: 1. Occurrence records underpin biodiversity analyses, but their coordinates are often erroneous or missing. Misplaced coordinates distort environmental predictors and range estimates used in conservation assessment. Existing tools flag suspect records or georeference locality text, but rarely correct coordinates, provide calibrated uncertainty, or quantify downstream consequences. 2. We present GeoMend, a deterministic, rule-based method that flags and corrects suspect coordinates and georeferences records lacking coordinates from locality text, assigning each a precision tier or uncertainty radius. It uses no machine learning or artificial intelligence. We evaluate it against expert coordinates for 16,913 records and 736 species on Hispaniola, compare georeferencers using 5,000 localities from 72 countries, and measure changes in environmental predictors and the extent of occurrence. 3. On held-out Hispaniola records, GeoMend flags 92% of coordinates more than 5 km from expert truth, versus 27% for CoordinateCleaner. Among the accepted corrections with paired coordinates, the median error falls from 2.19 to 0.82 km, and 68% of the complete held-out pairs improve. On records placed by both GeoMend and GEOLocate that also have original coordinates, the median error is 0.67 km for GeoMend versus 10.69 km for GEOLocate. For records lacking coordinates, evaluated uncertainty radii contain expert truth about 92% of the time in well-supported gazetteer classes. Correction reduces the mean standardized environmental distance from expert truth by 38% and moves the extent of occurrence toward expert truth by a median of 8% (mean of 79%). Corrections and newly georeferenced records give 17 Hispaniola species their first range estimate. 4. On the global benchmark, GeoMend is more accurate than GPT-4o for two-thirds of the records placed by all four comparators, with median errors of 4.4 and 10.8 km, respectively. Applied to Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) records lacking coordinates, it places records from 82,180 previously unmapped species across 233 countries, ranging from precise locality interpretations to administrative centroids. Automated placement makes the global backlog more approachable, while explicit tiers distinguish uses supported by precise and coarse coordinates. Further georeferencing requires regional expertise to combine automated placement with local knowledge.

title: Scents for safe sex: a volatile sex pheromone promotes outbreeding in a parasitoid wasp with severe genetic load
content: When mating among genetically related individuals results in inbreeding depression, various behaviors and life-history traits evolve to favor outbreeding. Long-range sexual communication following natal dispersal is one such adaptation. In parasitoid wasps with single-locus complementary sex determination (sl-CSD), inbreeding increases the production of unviable or sterile diploid males. Mastrus ridens is such a species, with a genetic load underpinned by sl-CSD, combined with a high potential for sibmating because siblings emerge in close proximity from the same host and become sexually active shortly after emergence. With this context in mind, we investigated the mate-finding strategy of M. ridens using complementary behavioral, chemical, and electrophysiological approaches. Wind-tunnel bioassays and field experiments showed that males orient toward virgin females and, to a lesser extent, mated females. This attraction from a distance appeared to be the sole form of conspecific attraction. Chemical analyses using static and dynamic headspace sampling and solvent extracts, followed by GC-MS, revealed several potential pheromonal candidates, including methyl 6-methylsalicylate. This compound elicited reproducible antennal responses in males in GC-EAD recordings. Altogether, our results suggest that mate finding in M. ridens is guided by a volatile sex pheromone emitted by females, with methyl 6-methylsalicylate as one putative component. Such mate-finding mechanisms promote outbreeding and may explain the low proportion of unfit diploid males observed in natural populations. Surprisingly, chemical analyses suggested that males also emit this compound, whereas neither males nor females showed behavioral responses to males. This apparent discrepancy suggests that attraction may depend on a more complex pheromonal signal and opens further avenues for investigation.

title: Piloting floral-visitor assemblages: Camera-based monitoring in Physoplexis comosa (Campanulaceae), a cliff-dwelling Eastern Alpine endemic Physoplexis comosa (Campanulaceae)
content: Understanding floral visitor dynamics along elevational gradients is essential for assessing potential implications for pollen limitation and population genetic processes in fragmented populations of cliff-dwelling alpine endemics. Physoplexis comosa (Campanulaceae) is a chasmophytic paleoendemic restricted to vertical rock faces on dolomitic and limestone bedrock from 200 to 2,800 m a.s.l. The species exhibits a specific floral morphology with fused corolla apices, basal openings for nectar access, and secondary pollen presentation, yet its functional floral visitor assemblage has remained poorly characterized across the species' elevational range. In this pilot study, we tested a two-tier camera-monitoring setup combining action cameras for diurnal monitoring with Raspberry Pi-based systems equipped with IR illumination for combined diurnal and nocturnal recording. We conducted monitoring across five elevational sites (1,480 to 2,400 m a.s.l.) in the Eastern Alps. Recorded video material was downsampled and annotated using the Addax platform alongside manual cross-validation to record physical contact events. Preliminary results confirm the technical feasibility of continuous monitoring in steep terrain and suggest possible elevational variation in diurnal visitors, alongside nocturnal activity by Geometridae moths. Camera-based observations provided higher functional resolution and revealed a different visitor assemblage than previous eDNA metabarcoding trials. This proof-of-concept establishes a methodological foundation for forthcoming multi-day monitoring campaigns and complements ongoing studies of the mating system and population-genetic analyses.

title: From Recovery to Risk: Intensifying ENSO Events Drive Extirpation Risk in a Marine Predator
content: Climate change poses a major threat to marine mammal populations, many of which remain vulnerable after years of overexploitation during the 17th to 20th centuries. Extreme climate events have grown in both frequency and severity in recent decades, and this trend is projected to accelerate under continued greenhouse gas emissions. Here, we assess how this intensification affects a top marine predator at the epicentre of extreme El Nino events - the Peruvian population of Otaria byronia (South American sea lion). We first apply a Bayesian population model that best predicts observed population dynamics to reconstruct female O. byronia population trends, estimate vital rates, and evaluate the effects of environmental drivers on survival and reproduction. We then use the same model to project extirpation risk under multiple future climate scenarios reflecting anticipated increases in both the intensity and frequency of extreme El Nino events. Our reconstruction reveals that the Peruvian O. byronia population has shown considerable resilience to episodic El Nino events over the past quarter-century, likely sustained by high female survival during normal and favourable years. However, under a scenario of moderate increases in El Nino frequency and intensity, the probability of extirpation over the next 50 years is 83.4% higher than under current conditions. As disturbance regimes intensify globally, we suggest that resilience-oriented management frameworks, grounded in species-specific demographic data and environmental context, as demonstrated here, will be essential for safeguarding marine mammal populations against an increasingly volatile climate.

title: Zoogeochemical engineers: Galapagos giant tortoises link terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems through sediment transport and nutrient dynamics
content: Animal movements can transport materials across ecosystem boundaries, while simultaneously modifying habitats through physical engineering. We integrated GPS telemetry, camera trapping, sediment measurements and physicochemical sampling of ponds on Santa Cruz Island, Galapagos, to evaluate how giant tortoises connect and shape terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems. Telemetry revealed 2,254 visits by 21 tortoises to 12 ponds, with visits lasting up to 21.38 h and showing strong seasonal and diel variation, while camera traps showed peak pond use in January and during early morning and late afternoon. Greater tortoise abundance was associated with higher ammonium, dissolved organic carbon and total phosphorus concentrations, while ponds with persistently greater tortoise abundance had higher total suspended solids. Departing tortoises carried a mean 505.9 g of sediment, yielding a conservative potential export of 8.20 kg per tortoise per year and tens of tonnes annually. These findings identify giant tortoises as mobile zoogeochemical engineers linking terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems through physical and biogeochemical pathways.

title: Edge-enhanced disruptive camouflage is contrast dependent in VR environments
content: In camouflage research, field studies provide ecological validity but lack experimental control, and computer-based experimental studies have the opposite issue. Virtual reality (VR) systems could potentially allow researchers to have both experimental control and ecological validity. Here we develop a VR environment using Unreal Engine and present it via a head-mounted display (HMD). The HMD affords binocular depth and therefore a more ecologically valid, three-dimensional environment, whilst still maintaining experimental control. Disruptive camouflage interferes with depth-based cues, making it a good candidate for testing within a VR environment. Disruptively camouflaged moth-like targets were presented to human surrogate predators, and their survivability was measured. We show that VR can be used to measure camouflage effectiveness by replicating existing findings showing that edge-enhanced disruptive camouflage (EE-DC) is more effective than disruptive camouflage (DC) alone. Furthermore, we extend these findings to show that the effectiveness of EE-DC is modulated by the relative contrast of the disruptive patches. Specifically, it is more effective when the contrast difference between the patches is low. Additionally, we considered edge-enhancement in isolation and found that it still provided a camouflage benefit even without a DC component. Search paradigms within an immersive VR experimental framework offer a unique opportunity to evaluate camouflage theory in a rigorous, yet ecologically grounded manner.

title: Forward time-series causal inference based on forest weights and conditional dependence
content: Unveiling directional causality in complex, high-dimensional dynamical systems remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional nonparametric approaches, such as Convergent Cross Mapping, require computationally intensive surrogate tests and frequently yield false-positive detections under strong coupling due to generalized synchronization. Here, we present F-CODEC (Forest-weighted Conditional Dependence Coefficient), a forward-looking causal discovery framework integrating generalized random forests with adaptive rank conditioning. Nonparametrically conditioning on the target variable's intrinsic delay coordinates systematically neutralizes shared manifold representations, suppressing false positives without surrogate data. Furthermore, an analytical time-series threshold allows instant, rigorous hypothesis testing directly from raw observations. We demonstrate F-CODEC's resilience against generalized synchronization and high-dimensional noise across canonical chaotic benchmarks and multi-species network motifs. Applying F-CODEC to historical lynx-hare cycles resolves delayed trophic forcing, while in-situ IoT honeybee monitoring captures real-time microclimate-acoustic causal surges preceding colony-level behavioral events. F-CODEC establishes a practical, scalable, and surrogate-free tool for causal discovery in nonlinear dynamical systems.

title: Carabid beetle communities along a gradient of agroecological systems: disentangling the roles of pesticides and soil tillage
content: The potential of alternative agricultural systems, such as organic or conservation agriculture, for biodiversity restoration has been widely investigated.
