However, variability of practices within each of these two categories of agricultural system has rarely been accounted for. Furthermore, these systems have most often been studied separately, isolating either organic or conservation agriculture (itself often reduced to a soil tillage reduction), and rarely analyzing these systems side by side. This study attempts to disentangle these multiple interrelationships by sampling carabid beetles in a network of 48 commercial Belgian farms including organic agriculture (OA), conservation agriculture (CA), farms combining the two approaches (OCA) and farms applying conventional practices (CVA). In each farm, we sampled carabids using pitfall and emergence traps in one winter cereal field and collected a detailed description of crop management practices. We found that community composition was primarily structured by seasonality early in the season (March, April) followed by convergence (May, June) driven by the aggregation of the most dominant species. Based on agroecosystem classification, organic certification (i.e., the absence of synthetic pesticide use) exerted a twofold stronger effect than application of conservation agriculture principles (i.e., reduced or no soil tillage) on carabid beetle community composition. Notably, OCA supported carabid assemblages that were structurally distinct from those of CA and CVA. Furthermore, carabid communities associated with OA differed significantly in composition from those of CVA. Observed and estimated species richness were also significantly higher in OCA than in CA and CVA, while OA differed from CVA only for observed richness. Beyond differences among agricultural systems, community responses were associated with specific management practices, which explained nearly a quarter of the compositional variation with significant influence of the duration since organic conversion and the frequency of synthetic pesticide application. Carabid abundances were negatively affected by synthetic pesticides and moldboard ploughing, whereas richness was more strongly related to the time since conversion to OA, cover crops, and organic amendments. Overall, these results position synthetic inputs and time since conversion as the main filters over carabid communities. Our study highlights the importance of jointly considering system level analyses and detailed management practices to better understand the complex relationships between agricultural practices and carabid communities.

title: Fluffy nests and bloody parasites: feather lining does not mitigate bird blow flies infestations
content: Feathers incorporated into bird nests are thought to provide multiple benefits, including thermal insulation and protection against nest-dwelling ectoparasites. For instance, in Swallows, it has been suggested that feathers influence infestations by Protocalliphora blow flies either by acting as a physical barrier between larvae and nestlings or through chemical compounds associated with preen oil. However, empirical evidence for an antiparasitic effect of feathers remains equivocal. Using 1,100 naturally infested Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) nests collected from a nest-box study system monitored in southern Quebec, Canada, between 2004 and 2018, we tested whether nest mass and feather abundance influenced hematophagous ectoparasites (Protocalliphora spp.) loads. We further assessed whether feather abundance directly affected body size using measurements of 1,513 P. sialia puparia, and emergence success using data from 961 Protocalliphora spp. puparia. Nest mass was positively associated with feather abundance, and both variables showed very weak positive relationships with parasite abundance. Feather abundance was unrelated to puparium size nor parasite emergence success. Our results provide no support for an anti-parasitic effect of feather lining within Tree Swallow nests. Using one of the largest datasets assembled to date on feather-lined nests and avian blow flies, we found no evidence that feather abundance impairs Protocalliphora density, development or emergence success. However, our findings do not preclude potential effects of feathers on other ectoparasites or microorganisms with different life histories. Future studies simultaneously monitoring multiple parasite taxa (such as fleas, mites, or bacteria) may therefore be needed to fully evaluate the ecological consequences of feather lining within avian nests.

title: SELECTIVE SURVIVAL OF AVIAN ECTOPARASITES IN AGROINTENSIVE HABITATS AND SUBSEQUENT EFFECTS ON HOST SELECTION BY PARASITOIDS
content: Morphological variation in insects can indicate responses to habitat change and land use intensification, with potential consequences for trophic interactions. In insect host-parasitoid systems, host body is often a key determinant of offspring development and emergence success, as well as parasitoid host-selection behavior. Yet, most studies in agricultural landscapes have focused on size variation in crop-associated insects (i.e.: pests, pollinators and enemies), leaving those relying on non-crop resources largely unexplored. Here, we investigated how agroenvironmental contexts and trophic resource availability influence puparial size in Protocalliphora sialia (Diptera: Calliphoridae), an obligate hematophagous ectoparasite of Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) nestlings. We further tested whether puparial size affects emergence probability and risk of parasitoidism by Nasonia spp. (Hymenoptera: Pteromalidae) jewel wasps. Using 1,513 P. sialia puparia from 88 nests within a nest-box monitoring system spanning a 10,200-km^2 east-west intensification gradient in southern Quebec, Canada, we evaluated how agrointensive contexts, avian host availability, and ectoparasite densities influence puparial size, parasitoidism risk, and emergence success. The agricultural context appears to shape puparial size through survival biases and/or altered growth rates. In agroextensive contexts (i.e.: pastures, forages with high tree cover), where Protocalliphora are more numerous, P. sialia puparia were smaller and exhibited greater size variation. Conversely, in agrointensive environments (maize and soybeans monocultures with higher doses of pesticides), where Protocalliphora are fewer, small individuals were underrepresented, suggesting a selective mortality in P. sialia population. However, puparial size explained less than 10% of the variation in emergence or parasitism, likely reflecting consistently high parasitic pressure from Nasonia wasps, which infested 50-90% of puparia, depending on site and year. Our findings highlight the importance of selective mortality in structuring trait distributions and modulating multi-trophic interactions in human-modified landscapes.

title: Baseline growth rate shapes pollutant impacts in aquatic environments: Evidence from antibiotic responses in the harmful cyanobacterium Microcystis
content: Hormesis is an important consideration in chemical risk assessment across most aquatic environments. Evidence suggests that hormetic responses are shaped by organismal physiological processes. Accordingly, predictions of hormesis under environmentally realistic conditions should account for physiological traits. Yet the role of these traits remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how baseline growth rate modulates antibiotic responses in the harmful cyanobacterium Microcystis and the underlying mechanisms. Results showed that at an antibiotic concentration of 200 ng L-1 (representing environmental concentration levels), slow-growing Microcystis populations exhibited an obvious growth enhancement more than 4-fold greater than that of fast-growing populations, and this enhancement was positively correlated with cellular reserves. A baseline growth rate below 0.19 day-1 emerged as the threshold below which hormetic responses were consistently observed. This study provides pioneering insights into how organisms' physiological states influence pollutant-induced hormetic responses in aquatic environments. Our findings point to a central principle for extrapolation that laboratory-derived toxicological responses may not translate directly to the field unless key physiological traits of the organisms are explicitly considered. In this regard, baseline growth rate and energy reserves may be key physiological traits for reliably predicting toxic effects at the population level. This study also makes an initial attempt to conceptualize a physiology-anchored framework for strengthening risk assessment of low-level emerging contaminants.

title: Hierarchical permutation entropy regression identifies decadal decline in the intrinsic predictability of butterfly populations
content: Short-term population dynamics are shaped by both external environmental stochasticity and endogenous ecological dynamics. The extent to which population trajectories maintain predictable temporal structure reflects underlying determinism and sets limits on inherent forecastability. Permutation entropy quantifies this intrinsic predictability using the relative frequency of short fluctuation motifs. However, requirements for long timeseries have restricted ecological applications. Here, I introduce a Bayesian hierarchical regression framework, incorporating entropy-neutral priors, that estimates expected permutation entropy from shorter, spatially-distributed ecological datasets. I validate the approach's capacity to detect the impact of increasing environmental variance through simulations. Applied to four decades of UK butterfly data, the approach identified increasing permutation entropy across 35 species, consistent with an increasing role of stochastic weather events. Outlier weather events did not have a consistent relationship with permutation entropy, highlighting the potential for environmental forcing to both disrupt and constrain trajectories. With this flexible approach, permutation entropy offers complementary perspectives on longstanding questions around forecasting and population dynamics.

title: Functional Diversity of Reef Fishes in the Veracruz Reef System National Park, SW Gulf of Mexico
content: Reef fish assemblages in the Veracruz Reef System National Park (VRSNP) are strongly structured along a pronounced north-south gradient, where environmental conditions, urban proximity, and protection levels interact to shape functional diversity and ecosystem functioning. This gradient creates contrasting ecological conditions between northern and southern reefs, providing a natural framework for evaluating how spatial variation influences resilience. Using a stationary visual census across ten reefs distributed latitudinally, we quantified functional entities based on six ecological traits and calculated functional richness, redundancy, over-redundancy, vulnerability, specialization, and originality. A two-way permutational ANOVA and redundancy analysis were used to detect spatial and temporal patterns and to link functional indices with environmental features. The southern sector displayed the most intense functional shifts. Nearshore southern reefs, strongly exposed to sedimentation, nutrient loading, and physical disturbance, exhibited reduced functional richness, fewer functional entities, and high functional vulnerability, indicating strong environmental filtering. Over time, these reefs shifted toward generalist-dominated assemblages with rising redundancy, suggesting functional convergence. In contrast, southern offshore reefs supported higher taxonomic and functional richness, buffered by greater habitat complexity and distance from shore, although they showed declining redundancy, likely reflecting sensitivity to regional climatic disturbances. In the northern sector, the gradient was moderated by effective protection, which reshaped functional configurations. Nearshore protected reefs such as Isla Sacrificios and Isla de Enmedio maintained high redundancy, low vulnerability, and high biomass of large-bodied fishes, resembling offshore systems rather than disturbed southern nearshore reefs. The northern offshore reef (Isla Verde) shared some of these attributes but exhibited temporal declines in richness, signaling emerging vulnerabilities along the gradient. Functional originality and specialization aligned with benthic states across the gradient, particularly where macroalgal or calcareous substrates prevailed. Overall, the north-south gradient is the primary axis of functional organization in VRSNP, revealing that resilience emerges from the interplay among reef geomorphology, urban influence, and governance effectiveness.

title: Conceptualising and quantifying phenological plasticity through latent responses to seasonal environmental progression
content: Quantifying how individuals adjust the seasonal timings of life-history events (i.e. their phenology) in response to seasonal environmental conditions is fundamental to predicting impacts of changing seasonality. However, the current standard approach of inferring phenological responses by directly analysing observed event dates relies on foundational assumptions that could be invalidated by changing seasonality, and excludes individuals that do not express focal events, potentially generating misleading inferences. To overcome these limitations, we devised a Phenological Threshold Model (PTM) that conceptualizes phenological events as switches between discrete life-history states and primarily estimates variation in underlying latent dynamic responses to seasonal progression, from which event dates secondarily arise. We demonstrate that the PTM can accurately retrieve simulated parameter values, including given incomplete seasonal field observations. Application to multi-year data on annual breeding in black-legged kittiwakes (Rissa tridactyla) demonstrated substantial among-individual variation in latent responses to seasonally varying environmental drivers, and associated daily probabilities that individuals will initiate breeding, revealing how annual distributions of breeding dates and proportions of non-breeders jointly arise. We thereby formalise a new conceptual and statistical framework for quantifying the potential for, and constraints on, rapid plastic and micro-evolutionary changes in phenology in changing seasonal climatic and environmental regimes.

title: Burrow disturbance, renovation, and collapse in a cavity-nesting seabird
content: Researcher disturbance can alter the behavior, survival, and breeding success of wildlife, with effects that are especially well-documented in waterbirds. Anecdotal reports suggest that disturbance can even cause cavity-nesting species to alter the structure of their nests. We used a long-term study of a burrowing seabird, the Leach's Storm-Petrel (Hydrobates leucorhous), to ask whether storm-petrels renovate existing burrows and whether such renovation is related to a history of researcher disturbance. Our study was conducted at the Bowdoin Scientific Station on Kent Island, New Brunswick, Canada, where in 2024 we measured the burrow architecture of 363 burrows, including length and structure for occupied and unoccupied burrows both inside and outside a long-term study site with consistent research activity. Of these, 150 burrows had been measured in 2006, allowing for direct longitudinal comparison of burrow architecture. Nearly all burrows changed in length over the 18-year study period (mean absolute change = 20.8 cm +- 18.2 SD). A linear model revealed two contrasting processes of burrow length change: more frequently occupied burrows grew longer, whereas initially longer burrows shortened towards mean burrow length (~50 cm) through collapse. Occupied burrows inside the long-term study site were on average 34% longer and significantly more complex than burrows adjacent to the site, suggesting that researcher disturbance directly or indirectly reshapes burrows. Overall, these results show that storm-petrel burrows are shaped by cycles of renovation and subsequent collapse that may be exacerbated by human disturbance. Given ongoing population declines in storm-petrels and other cavity-nesting seabirds, this study emphasizes the need to balance scientific research with minimizing disturbance, particularly in long-term studies.

title: Carnivores in a metropolitan forest island: first spatial capture-recapture estimates reveal high densities of leopards and striped hyenas in Jaipur, India
content: Urban protected areas (PAs) have become important habitats for wildlife in rapidly expanding human-dominated landscapes. These PAs may provide refuge and continuously abundant resources, which may enable some adaptable carnivores to persist and attain high abundances. However, little is known about the population ecology and interactions between carnivores sharing such spatially restricted and disturbed urban habitats. We evaluated the densities and spatio-temporal interactions of leopards (Panthera pardus) and striped hyenas (Hyaena hyaena) in Jhalana-Amagarh Conservation Reserve, a protected area (PA) embedded within the metropolis of Jaipur, India. During May-July 2025, we deployed 30 paired camera-traps and used spatially explicit capture-recapture models to estimate density and individual activity centres. We further quantified their diel activity and temporal overlap using kernel density estimation. Leopard density was estimated at 7.03 {+/-} 1.31 individuals/10 km sq and striped hyena density at 4.06 {+/-} 0.96 individuals/10 km sq, with activity centres of both species occurring in close proximity and frequently towards the reserve periphery. Both species were predominantly nocturnal and showed high temporal overlap ({Delta}4 = 0.801, CI=0.73-0.86). Our results report exceptionally high leopard and striped hyena densities in an urban PA and exemplify the importance of small PAs within rapidly expanding cities, stressing the need for finer-scale studies more broadly to understand the mechanisms shaping interactions between the two species. However, such systems require careful management of food subsidies, habitat quality and connectivity along with long-term monitoring of population viability, disease dynamics and human-wildlife conflict.

title: Priority effects influence bacterial community assembly on temperate deciduous tree leaves
content: Microbial community assembly on leaves (the phyllosphere) is influenced by deterministic, stochastic, and historical processes. However, the importance of historical processes such as priority effects, where the timing and order of colonization influence community assembly, has not been extensively investigated in field-based phyllosphere studies. We designed a field experiment in a temperate forest in Quebec where we inoculated five strains of Methylobacterium onto the leaves of red maple and American beech trees, either early or late during the growing season. We quantified microbial community structure throughout the season using metabarcoding of a Methylobacterium-targeting rpoB primer as well as a 16S rRNA primer targeting the entire bacterial community. We show that the effects of inoculation on bacterial communities depend on inoculation timing: early-season inoculation led to strain-specific shifts in community composition, while late-season inoculation had no significant effect. Although the effect of early-season inoculation weakened over time, early- and late-season inoculation still led to different community compositions at the end of the growing season. Our study demonstrates that priority effects contribute to the assembly of phyllosphere bacterial communities under field conditions, with arrival timing and strain identity shaping community trajectories. Considering historical processes will thus be crucial for successful microbiome management.

title: Large and persistent social risks to forest carbon projects
content: Despite the popularity of carbon credits as a tool to offset greenhouse gas emissions, there are growing concerns over whether their climate mitigation claims are robust. Most attention has focused on natural risks to forest carbon projects, such as wildfire, while social risks (e.g., those driven by fraud, mismanagement, and land conflicts) remain largely unquantified. Here we analyze 244 forest-based carbon projects to assess the vulnerability of the voluntary carbon market to social risks and find that projects systematically underestimate their risk of failure. Even under optimistic assumptions, projects are roughly twice as likely to fail within 25 years as their self-assessed risk implies over a 100-year horizon. Projecting these trends forward, we show that credits issued to failed projects could exceed the reserves registries hold to mitigate these risks within 1-2 decades. Overall, our results suggest stronger mechanisms and reserves are needed to ensure carbon credits deliver the promised climate benefits.

title: Determining Spatial Patterns of Human-Tiger and Human-Leopard Conflict across South Asia through A Multi-Scale Regional Approach
content: Over the past two decades, significant population recoveries of tigers and leopards have driven a substantial rise in human-carnivore conflict across South Asia. Sustaining the long-term conservation of both species demands effective, adaptive conflict management. However, existing research is largely confined to isolated landscapes or protected areas, hindering the identification of spatial conflict drivers across broader, heterogeneous regions. To address this gap, this study compiled 4,457 human leopard conflict (HLC) and 2,563 human tiger conflict (HTC) records spanning 2000 to 2024 across Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, and Nepal. We evaluated conflict locations against 33 landscape, anthropogenic, climatic, topographic, and hydrological predictors across three spatial scales using binomial generalized linear regression models and three alternative background sampling methods. Model performance peaked at the largest spatial scale for both species and remained consistent across sampling strategies. HTC correlated positively with forest fragmentation and proximity to human settlements, but decreased with higher overall anthropogenic disturbance. Conversely, HLC concentrated in highly productive, high-precipitation, human-modified landscapes. These contrasting spatial patterns highlight distinct ecological responses to habitat modification and carry unique conservation implications. Ultimately, this study underscores the need to integrate carnivore abundance, wild prey densities, and socioeconomic factors to achieve a holistic understanding of conflict dynamics.

title: Effects of Heat Shock and Smoke on the Germination of Woody Species from Tropical Dry Forests
content: Fire-dependent or fire-influenced ecosystems harbor species with diverse response strategies, such as smoke-stimulated germination and dormancy release through heat shocks. Although these cues influence germination in many fire-prone ecosystems, their effects on seeds of woody species from tropical dry forests (TDFs) remain poorly understood. We evaluated the germination response of twelve TDF woody species to three heat-shock temperatures (80, 120, and 160C), two exposure times (3 and 5 min), and two smoke conditions (with and without smoke water), plus dry and wet controls. We also assessed the relationship between germination and functional seed traits, including permeability, seed-coat thickness, mass, and shape index. Of the eleven species that germinated, four showed broad tolerance, with no significant reduction in germination even at 160C for 5 min, which was associated with lower permeability, thicker seed coats, and greater mass. Four other species showed restricted tolerance to heat, with significant declines in germination at higher temperatures or longer exposure times, and were associated with higher permeability, thinner seed coats, and lower seed mass. The remaining three species showed heat-stimulated germination between 80 and 120C and tended to have lower shape-index values. Smoke treatments significantly increased germination in three species, Ceiba pentandra, Guazuma ulmifolia, and Samanea saman. In the remaining species, significant differences were either absent or attributable to moisture or imbibition effects rather than to smoke itself. Overall, germination responses to heat were associated with variation in functional seed traits, whereas responses to smoke were less widespread and showed a less consistent functional pattern.

title: Spiders as natural DNA samplers recover arthropod community diversity and biotic interactions across space and time
content: Global arthropod decline demands effective biodiversity monitoring strategies. However, most current monitoring approaches do not provide an exhaustive picture of arthropod community structure. In particular, biotic interactions and temporal patterns of biodiversity change are still poorly understood. Here we explore the possibility of addressing these two shortfalls using spiders, one of the most important predators of terrestrial arthropods, as natural samplers for arthropod community DNA. We conducted several experiments comparing the recovered community composition between spider gut contents and traditional monitoring methods. Additionally, we used archived spiders from long-term collections to assess the preservation of prey DNA over time. Spiders proved to be highly efficient natural DNA samplers, with gut content metabarcoding revealing similar community composition and alpha- and beta-diversity like traditional methods. Unique arthropod taxa were detected by spider gut contents and traditional methods respectively, indicating that these two approaches can serve as valuable complements to each other. Well-preserved archived spiders effectively reconstructed historical diets up to 20 years back in time, showing that historical spider collections can act as time capsules of the wider diversity that occurred in the spider's habitat. Spiders as natural samplers overcome critical shortfalls in biodiversity monitoring and contribute to our future understanding of community assembly across space and time.

title: Movement mechanisms explain current animal density patterns and predict their reorganization under global change
content: Aim: To test whether individual movement mechanisms inferred from animal tracking data can be scaled up to explain landscape-scale patterns of population density and improve predictions of population redistribution under future environmental change. Location: Texas Gulf Coast, USA Time Period: 2009-2018 Major Taxa Studied: Whooping Crane (Grus americana) Methods: We parameterized individual-level step-selection functions using 14,898 GPS locations from 22 Whooping Cranes and propagated the resulting movement and habitat-selection mechanisms across the landscape to derive steady-state distributions of space use. We compared these movement-informed predictions with correlative species distribution models fitted to the same data. Predictions were evaluated using withheld tracking observations and fully independent population-level aerial-survey data. We then projected both approaches under sea-level-rise scenarios to assess how future habitat loss and fragmentation alter crane space use. Results: Movement mechanisms derived from individual-level tracking data captured the mechanistic dependence of population density on habitat quality and spatial configuration. When projected across the landscape, these mechanisms reproduced fully independently observed density patterns and outperformed conventional species distribution models. Because predictions arose from movement mechanisms rather than occurrence-environment correlations, movement-informed models also captured the effects of habitat reconfiguration under sea-level rise. They projected pronounced population redistribution and an expansion of core space-use areas of up to 80% which conventional models missed. Main Conclusions: Individual movement mechanisms derived from biologging data can scale up to explain current population structure and predict future redistribution under environmental change. By mechanistically accounting for how habitat configuration constrains accessibility, movement-informed models reveal severe impacts of fragmentation that are missed by conventional distribution models. Rapidly expanding biologging datasets therefore offer a scalable basis for connecting individual behavior to macroecological patterns and improving biodiversity forecasts in changing landscapes.

title: A sampling-theory framework for richness-uniqueness relationships
content: Ecological uniqueness, commonly quantified by local contribution to beta diversity (LCBD), is important for understanding and conserving biodiversity. Its widely documented negative relationship with species richness has led to the view that species-poor communities may be disproportionately important for regional diversity. Here, we derive neutral expectations for richness-uniqueness relationships and show that negative slopes can arise from neutral assembly rather than necessarily reflecting an ecological signal of uniqueness. Neutral simulations validate the analytical expectations across abundance- and incidence-based LCBD formulations. Applying the framework to the Barro Colorado Island tropical forest and North American Breeding Bird Survey, we show that accounting for neutral sampling expectations substantially changes the ranking and spatial distribution of ecologically unique sites. By separating neutral sampling expectations from excess uniqueness, our framework provides a principled basis for interpreting ecological uniqueness and informing biodiversity conservation.

title: Two new gastropod holobionts from Atlantic hydrothermal vents showing different levels of endosymbiosis dependence
content: Chemosynthetic symbioses underpin animal life at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, encompassing substantial variabilities in symbiont identity, metabolic capacity, and host dependence. Here, we characterise symbioses in two peltospirid snails from Mid-Atlantic Ridge vents, Peltospira gargantua and P. smaragdina, using 3D anatomical reconstruction, stable isotope analyses, fluorescence in situ hybridization, transmission electron microscopy, and metagenomics. Both species hosted abundant intracellular Campylobacterota within bacteriocytes of a hypertrophied oesophageal gland. Their dominant symbionts belonged to genus Sulfurimonas, but the two hosts were associated with distinct symbiont lineages. Symbiont genomes encoded carbon fixation through the rTCA cycle, sulfide oxidation, and Group I Ni-Fe hydrogenases, indicating combined thiotrophic and hydrogenotrophic capacities. Hydrogenase copy number varied across vent fields from one to three copies. The P. gargantua symbiont from the hydrogen-enriched Hydra vent field carried two divergent copies, including one with a truncated catalytic region, potentially reflecting local adaptation to vent geochemistry. Anatomical and isotopic comparisons further revealed contrasting host dependence, with P. gargantua having a proportionally larger oesophageal gland and ventricle coupled with a reduced radula, as well as a greater nitrogen-isotope enrichment between symbiotic and non-symbiotic tissues. The smaller oesophageal gland and larger feeding apparatus of P. smaragdina point to it being mixotrophic. Previously, all known peltospirid symbioses have partnered with Gammaproteobacteria, and we expand the known diversity of peltospirid symbioses. Our findings underscore how closely related hosts can exhibit different degrees of dependence on symbiosis, and that mixotrophic symbiosis may be prevalent in small vent species previously thought to be non-symbiotic.

title: Similar fertility losses in response to heat are followed by distinct recovery trajectories across seven Drosophila species
content: Heat-induced sterility is widespread across ectotherm species, yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In mated females, thermal stress can disrupt female reproductive physiology while also affecting sperm stored within the reproductive tract, making the mechanisms of fertility loss difficult to distinguish. Here, we investigated the extent and recovery dynamics of female heat-induced fertility loss across seven Drosophila species. We tracked fertility after acute heat exposure, tested whether remating restored fertility, quantified stored sperm in two closely related species, and examined whether reproductive thermal sensitivity covaried with adult heat tolerance. We found that heat exposure reduced egg-hatching success in all seven species, but recovery differed among species. Fertility recovered within several days in most species, whereas D. simulans showed persistent declines and D. melanogaster showed limited recovery. Remating restored or maintained fertility in both species. Stored sperm declined through time in both D. simulans and D. mauritiana, but D. mauritiana retained more sperm at later sampling points, consistent with their contrasting patterns of fertility decline and maintenance. Across species, greater adult heat tolerance was associated with smaller immediate reductions in fertility, but not with cumulative reproductive loss across subsequent days. Together, these findings show that similar initial fertility losses can lead to markedly different recovery trajectories and highlight the importance of comparative, multi-species approaches that integrate female physiology, sperm-storage dynamics, mating behavior, and whole-organism thermal tolerance when assessing reproductive resilience to climate warming.

title: Heterotrophic succession of invertebrate assemblages on fallen guava fruits in a tropical grove
content: Fallen fleshy fruits are temporary resource patches that can support diverse but transient invertebrate assemblages, yet their successional dynamics remain poorly documented in tropical landscapes modified by human activity. We examined heterotrophic succession on fallen ripe guava fruits, Psidium guajava, in a tropical grove in Barasat, West Bengal, India. Eight fruits were placed in exposed and shaded microhabitats and followed from fresh to degraded stages over 22 days. Invertebrates were recorded using repeated scan sampling, and daily observations for each fruit were analysed for taxon richness, Shannon diversity, total peak relative abundance, community composition and indicator taxa associated with decomposition stages. Across 141 daily fruit observations, we recorded 44 invertebrate taxa. Taxon richness, Shannon diversity and total peak relative abundance were highest during fresh and pre rotten stages and declined sharply during post rotten and degraded stages. Decomposition stage was the strongest predictor of alpha diversity, resource use intensity and community composition, whereas differences between exposed and shaded microhabitats were weaker. Indicator taxa showed clear successional replacement: fresh fruits were associated with drosophilid and tephritid flies; fresh and pre rotten fruits with nitidulid beetles and ants; and later stages with collembolans, staphylinids, blattodeans and other taxa associated with detrital stages. Ants, especially Pheidole sp., were conspicuous resource users and showed guarding, hoarding, predation and pulp or seed removal behaviour, although their effects on other taxa remain observational. These results show that fallen guava fruits function as ephemeral heterotrophic resource patches, supporting rapid invertebrate turnover at fine temporal scales in a tropical grove.

title: Machine Learning Identification of Functional Trait Syndromes Associated with Responsiveness to Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi
content: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are widespread plant symbionts that enhance nutrient acquisition, growth, and stress tolerance, yet plant responsiveness to AMF varies substantially and remains difficult to predict. We developed Trait2Myco, a Random Forest based machine-learning framework that integrates plant functional traits and environmental variables to predict mycorrhizal growth response (MGR). The framework was trained using 80 observations spanning four grass species grown under four precipitation regimes. Predictor variables included leaf and root economic traits together with precipitation, while total MGR served as the response variable. A full model incorporating ten functional traits and precipitation was trained using 80% of observations and evaluated on an independent testing dataset (20%, n = 16). The full model explained 41% of variation in MGR (R2 = 0.41), whereas a reduced ecological model containing only specific leaf area, specific root area, root carbon concentration, and precipitation improved predictive performance and explained 51.7% of variation (R2 = 0.517). Ten-fold cross-validation of the full model yielded an R2 of 0.983, RMSE of 0.046, and MAE of 0.036. Variable importance analysis identified specific leaf area, precipitation, root carbon concentration, and specific root area as the strongest predictors of responsiveness. Partial dependence analysis revealed nonlinear relationships between these predictors and MGR, while principal component analysis showed that highly responsive plants occupied distinct regions of functional trait space characterized by resource-acquisitive trait syndromes. Leaf and root traits contributed nearly equally to model performance, accounting for 41.9% and 41.3% of cumulative importance, respectively, while environmental factors contributed 16.8%. An exploratory analysis using an independent AMF colonization dataset produced similarly strong predictive relationships, suggesting that trait-based machine-learning approaches may generalize across multiple AMF-associated responses. Trait2Myco provides a reproducible framework for identifying plant trait syndromes associated with responsiveness to AMF and offers a practical tool for predicting mycorrhizal benefits across environmental gradients.

title: Scale matters: the arbuscular mycorrhiza - root hair trade-off from individual plants to communities
content: 1. Plant roots employ multiple strategies to acquire soil resources, including the outgrowth of root hairs and the association with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF). These structures represent alternative pathways to access soil resources. Evidence is derived mostly from studies within single species or multi-species experiments under controlled conditions. It remains unclear whether this trade-off holds under natural conditions and whether it manifests consistently across different scales of biological organization. 2. We analysed 81 grassland species representing grasses, forbs and legumes, sampled under heterogeneous field conditions in three regions across Germany, allowing for analyses (i) across different species (interspecific), (ii) across communities (intercommunity), (iii) within plant species (intraspecific) and (iv) within root systems of individual plants (intra-individual). Fine root traits related to AMF colonization (including scoring of fungal hyphae and arbuscules) and root hair growth (including length and incidence) were quantified. 3. Comparing plant species, we observed a strong negative correlation between mycorrhizal colonization and root hair traits, confirming previous studies working under controlled conditions. The negative relationship between root hair length and mycorrhization was also evident when comparing mean trait values at the plant community scale. Among different individuals of the same species (i.e. intraspecific scale), there was no consistent pattern of trait-trait relationship. When comparing within roots of the same plant (i.e. intra-individual scale), co-occurrence of root hairs and mycorrhiza was less likely than what would be expected by chance, with forbs showing the most consistent negative pattern. 4. Our study demonstrates that the hypothesized trade-off between AMF and root hairs is a robust pattern under field conditions at the community and interspecific scale. At the intraspecific scale, no uniform trade-off pattern can be discerned, and within single root systems the negative trade-off pattern is widespread but weak. This indicates that ecological and evolutionary constraints shape trait-trait relationships at higher scale, whereas physiological limits do not restrict trait co-occurrence at lower scales.

title: Hydrodynamics structure the physiological trajectory and bloom dynamics of a harmful diatom species across neighboring coastal ecosystems
content: Hydrodynamics is a strong regulator of phytoplankton cell densities and population connectivity. However, the extent to which hydrodynamics, specifically dilution and advection, dictates the internal physiological state and overall bloom dynamics remains poorly understood. We conducted an integrated study of the harmful diatom Pseudo-nitzschia australis in two neighboring coastal bays with similar abiotic conditions but contrasting bloom trajectories. Using a combination of field observations, transcriptomics, domoic acid (DA) measurements, and hydrodynamic simulations, we show that a three-fold difference in dilution rates alone explains a 25-day shift in bloom timing and an order-of-magnitude difference in cell densities. Transcriptomic profiling revealed distinct metabolic and stress-associated gene modules that synchronized with hydrodynamically-mediated nutrient depletion rate, linking residence times to cellular mortality. Furthermore, directional connectivity between the bays may explain population-level toxin heterogeneity, as advection of older cells, releasing DA outside the cells, may have decreased the proportion of intracellular DA in the destination bay. Our results illustrate that hydrodynamics do not merely modulate population transport; they structure the full physiological life cycle of a bloom, from initiation to nutrient-driven demise. This highlights the necessity of considering hydrodynamics as a primary explanation for bloom dynamics with cascading effects on bloom onset, cell density, nutrient consumption, cell physiology and mortality.
